## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}

*Agent stack focus for this chapter.*

_When is another token, candidate, check, or model call worth its cost?_

An agent that deliberates before acting pays latency and money for a better chance of success, whether it spends them on a longer derivation, more candidate patches, an extra check, or another model call. Each purchase answers a different question. More tokens re-examine what the prompt already holds, more candidates raise the chance that a good one sits somewhere in the pool, and only an executed check adds a fact the model did not have. None of them makes the returned answer correct, because a selector can return a plausible failure, and a search that optimizes against a flawed check finds the flaw faster than the fix. Deliberation is therefore a budgeted allocation problem with a stopping rule. The runtime decides where the next unit of work goes, how far a passing check can be trusted, and when to stop, abstain, or escalate instead of returning its best unverified guess. Every extra turn spent inside one decision lengthens the horizon, so that spending has to be bounded before the agent acts on anything.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Compare depth, breadth, and feedback as ways to spend a per-decision budget, by the information each adds, the tokens it consumes, and its critical path.
- Distinguish candidate availability from selected-output quality when evaluating voting, learned scoring, and task-specific checks.
- Calculate accepted-set precision from stated checker error rates and explain how adaptive search can change those assumptions.
- Represent a candidate plan as a dependency graph and identify which parts require revision after an observation changes.
- Analyze how step-level checks and pruning bound a search tree's growth and its scorer cost.
- Design stopping rules that enforce resource ceilings without treating budget exhaustion as acceptance evidence.
- Evaluate competing deliberation policies under a common budget and deadline by pass probability, actual spend, and abstentions.

:::

## Limits of a Single Response {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-insufficient-response}

The repair agent (@sec-vol3-intro-lighthouses) inspects the connection-pool implementation and receives a completed candidate patch. The invocation contract admits it as a candidate, yet the patch rests on an incomplete diagnosis. Client requests intermittently stall even after idle connections become available. Two distinct failure modes can produce this symptom: an aggressive timeout that aborts too early, or a lost notification when a worker thread returns a connection to the pool. When prompted, the language model proposes extending the timeout. That change offers a plausible workaround, but it provides no evidence that the timeout caused the stalls. Deploying such a patch immediately risks masking the latency tail while leaving the concurrency defect intact.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_h.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with the Horizon axis highlighted."}

*Deliberation extends the horizon with extra model turns and checks inside one decision, and hard ceilings bound that spend.*
:::

Before committing to an edit, the agent runtime can spend extra work in three distinct ways. It can give the model a longer output allowance to trace how threads acquire and release the lock step by step. It can sample several candidate patches that modify different parts of the pooling logic. It can also run a targeted test harness to record whether a waiting thread actually receives the condition-variable notification. Each option buys a different kind of evidence. Extended reasoning can expose logical flaws in the source text. Sampling across temperature or prompt variations can surface fixes that a greedy single pass misses. An instrumented test, by contrast, observes runtime state directly and reveals dynamic thread interactions that token generation alone cannot establish.

This division marks the boundary between model computation and runtime observation. Extra model computation re-evaluates information already present in the prompt. Within a single generation, a model can backtrack and revise an earlier analytical misstep even as the previous tokens remain frozen in its prefix. Pure computation, however, cannot create new empirical facts. Only an executed test reports how the running process behaves, and its conclusions hold only for the conditions and thread schedules that the test harness exercised.

Suppose the targeted test forces an interleaving where one worker thread waits while another returns a connection. The trace shows that the connection enters the pool, yet the waiting worker stays blocked past the notification point. That observation rules out the timeout hypothesis immediately and points the agent toward the signaling path. The agent can then write a patch that repairs the notification logic and test it against the failing reproducer. Passing a targeted reproducer still does not establish full task acceptance, because narrow tests can miss edge cases, and neither an unchecked hypothesis nor an isolated micro-test is enough to ship code to production. Even so, the two paths part ways before any file changes (@fig-vol3-diagnostic-tree). Acting on the first guess hides the symptom and keeps the defect, whereas checking first spends one short test to learn which hypothesis survives.

::: {#fig-vol3-diagnostic-tree fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Committing to a Hypothesis vs. Checking It**: Both paths start from the same connection-pool failure. On the left, generation builds on the timeout explanation without any observation that separates it from a missed notification, so the patch can hide the symptom while the defect remains. On the right, a targeted test orders a waiting worker and a returning connection, and its observation contradicts the timeout explanation before any edit. The revised candidate passes the reproducer, which still falls short of task acceptance." fig-alt="Two lanes below a box reading observed failure, request waits after a connection frees. The left lane, labeled commit first, holds H1 timeout too short with H2 missed notification drawn faded and dashed, then generate on H1 with no new evidence, then a timeout patch applied unchecked, ending in a red box reading symptom masked, notification defect remains. The right lane, labeled check first, holds both H1 and H2, then an amber targeted test observing the waiter still blocked after return, then the hypotheses again with H1 struck through and marked contradicted, then a notify on return patch, the revised candidate from H2, ending in a green box reading reproducer passes, acceptance still pending. A dashed horizontal line labeled first edit crosses both lanes: the left lane reaches it with no check, the right lane only after the test."}
![](images/svg/diagnostic_tree.svg)
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-probe-allocation
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PROBE AND GENERATION ALLOWANCES (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-03-probe-versus-generation.
# │ Goal: Compare a short diagnostic operation with an output allowance.
# │ Show: Generation time and output charge, distinct from probe duration.
# │ How: Reuse the registry weight-read allowance from Foundation Model;
# │      exclude prefill, queueing, transport, and probe setup overhead.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import BYTES_INT8, param

class ProbeAllocation:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    accel = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    answer_tokens = 1_024  # hypothetical output length
    probe_time = 0.040 * second  # hypothetical already-prepared test duration
    output_price = 15 * USD / 1_000_000  # hypothetical dollars per output token

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    weights = model.parameters / param * BYTES_INT8
    token_time = (weights / accel.memory.bandwidth).to(second)
    answer_time = answer_tokens * token_time
    answer_cost = answer_tokens * output_price
    time_ratio = answer_time / probe_time

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(answer_time > probe_time > 0 * second, "Positive scenario durations")
    check(answer_cost > 0 * USD, "Output has a positive scenario charge")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    answer_tokens_str = fmt_int(answer_tokens)
    probe_time_str = fmt_time(probe_time, unit="ms", precision=0)
    token_time_str = fmt_time(token_time, unit="ms", precision=2)
    answer_time_str = fmt_time(answer_time, unit="s", precision=2)
    answer_cost_str = fmt_usd(answer_cost, precision=5)
    output_price_str = fmt_usd(output_price * 1_000_000, precision=0)
    time_mult_str = fmt_multiple(time_ratio, precision=1)
```

::: {#nbk-03-probe-versus-generation .callout-notebook title="A probe vs. a longer answer"}

**Problem**: A prepared diagnostic test takes `{python} ProbeAllocation.probe_time_str`. A proposed explanation contains `{python} ProbeAllocation.answer_tokens_str` output tokens. How long does the explanation take to generate relative to the test?

**Variables**: The illustrative per-token generation time from @sec-vol3-foundation-model-per-call-work-estimate is `{python} ProbeAllocation.token_time_str`, derived from memory-bandwidth limits rather than a measured production service rate. The hypothetical output pricing is `{python} ProbeAllocation.output_price_str` per million tokens. Prompt processing, queueing, transport, test preparation, and the downstream model call that reads the test observation are excluded.

**Math**: Generating `{python} ProbeAllocation.answer_tokens_str` tokens at `{python} ProbeAllocation.token_time_str` per token requires `{python} ProbeAllocation.answer_time_str` and incurs `{python} ProbeAllocation.answer_cost_str` in token charges. Dividing this generation latency by the `{python} ProbeAllocation.probe_time_str` test run yields a factor of `{python} ProbeAllocation.time_mult_str`.

**Systems insight**: When the unresolved question concerns dynamic program behavior, the probe settles it `{python} ProbeAllocation.time_mult_str` faster than the model can generate a speculative explanation of it, and only the probe's answer is an observation. Running a test is preferable whenever its preparation and execution time remain below the explanation's `{python} ProbeAllocation.answer_time_str` and its outcome cleanly separates the competing failure modes. Conversely, an inconclusive test that does not separate the hypotheses provides no diagnostic gain regardless of its speed. Failure to reproduce can still supply negative evidence when the test's sensitivity to the suspected fault is known. A sound runtime spends work on whichever operation most cheaply removes the main source of uncertainty.

:::

The probe, and the decision to revise the patch on its evidence, both happened outside any single model call. The invocation contract of the previous chapter ends at one prompt and one candidate, accompanied only by metadata indicating whether generation reached a stop token or an output limit. That interface cannot decide whether the next second of latency or fraction of a cent is better spent on longer reasoning, extra candidate samples, or a runtime probe. An API response marked complete confirms only that generation finished, not that the proposed patch fixes the bug. **Test-time compute**\index{Test-time compute!definition} is all the system work the runtime orchestrates around the model call, with model weights held fixed, to generate, test, and select candidates before committing to an action. Governing that spend requires a runtime policy that sets hard ceilings on latency and cost, routes work across reasoning and checks, and stops cleanly without mistaking an exhausted budget for a verified solution.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The bounded single-invocation model contract is established in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-contract.
:::

Each part of that policy raises the next question. The runtime first chooses how to spend extra work across reasoning depth, candidate breadth, and empirical feedback (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-computation-allocation). Breadth produces a pool, so the runtime must then pick from it without being fooled by a plausible failure (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-candidate-diversity), and picking well depends on how far a passing check can be trusted (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-verification). When a check refutes a premise partway through a plan, the runtime should regenerate only what depended on it (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-planning-revision). Candidates and revisions together form a search whose spending must be tracked, reserved, and stopped (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-bounded-search), and the complete policy is finally judged against its alternatives under one budget and one deadline (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-strategy-design).

## Three Axes of Test-Time Compute {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-computation-allocation}

Giving a repair agent a four-thousand-token allowance does not determine its latency, memory footprint, or diagnostic reach, because the runtime can spend those same four thousand tokens on one long derivation, four parallel candidate patches, or three edit–test–revise rounds. Although all three options can consume the same number of output tokens, they stress the serving system in different ways. A long derivation generates tokens one after another along a single causal chain. Independent candidate patches can run concurrently across accelerator hardware. An edit–test–revise loop must pause model generation while each diagnostic test runs. Those dependencies determine which operations sit on the critical latency path and how much state the serving engine must hold in memory.

**Depth**\index{Depth axis!definition} extends sequential computation within a single candidate, **breadth**\index{Breadth axis!definition} explores multiple candidate paths concurrently, and **feedback**\index{Feedback axis!definition} folds environment observations into subsequent revisions. A **test-time deliberation rollout**\index{Test-time deliberation rollout!definition}\index{Deliberation|see{Test-time deliberation rollout}} is one bounded candidate-generation path, potentially interleaving verification checks and observation-driven revisions; the term comes from game search, where a rollout plays one line of moves forward to its end. Depth lengthens a rollout, breadth runs several in parallel, and feedback inserts checks between a rollout's turns. An allocation policy can combine all three: it might generate several candidate patches in parallel, run regression tests against each, and spend deeper step-by-step reasoning only on the most promising survivor. Throughout, model weights remain frozen, and every axis draws from the same test-time budget.

::: {#dfn-vol3-test-time-compute-budget .callout-definition title="Test-time compute budget"}

***Test-time compute budget***\index{Test-time compute budget!definition} is the per-decision allowance of processed prompt tokens, generated tokens, model invocations, verification checks, and elapsed wall-clock time that a runtime may expend, with model weights fixed, before it must select a candidate, abstain, or escalate to a human operator.

1.  **Significance**: The budget sets the attempt cost in the effective cost per accepted task, $\CostPerAcceptedTask = \mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]/\AcceptanceProbability$ (@eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task). Additional deliberation reduces cost per accepted task when it increases the acceptance rate $\AcceptanceProbability$ proportionally faster than it increases the expected attempt cost. A higher cost per accepted task can still be justified when it buys the required acceptance rate within the deadline (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-operating-point).
2.  **Distinction**: Training compute amortizes weight optimization once across all future tasks. Test-time compute recurs on every decision, where an internal reasoning allowance is merely one control surface alongside external tool invocations and verification checks.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating the maximum allocation ceiling as the expected spend, or treating an exhausted budget as evidence that the best remaining candidate is acceptable.

:::

What separates the three axes is their dependency structure (@fig-vol3-allocation-axes). Depth extends a single candidate through multi-step reasoning, breadth fans out to sampled candidates that converge on a selector, and feedback routes a candidate through a sandboxed check whose observation conditions the revision.

::: {#fig-vol3-allocation-axes fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Three compute allocation topologies**: Depth extends one candidate; breadth exposes separate sampled candidate paths followed by selection; feedback makes a later candidate depend on an observed check result. The arrows show dependencies, not guaranteed latency, cost, or correctness." fig-alt="Three panels labeled Depth, Breadth, and Feedback. Depth connects an input through a single chain of four reasoning segments to a candidate. Breadth fans an input out to three separate two-segment sample paths, bracketed as sampled paths, that converge on a selector, which outputs a candidate. Feedback sends a candidate into a dashed sandbox region containing a check, which produces an observation; a revised candidate receives one arrow from the observation and one from the original candidate."}
![](images/svg/three_compute_allocation_axes.svg)
:::

### Extending reasoning along the depth axis {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-depth-axis}

Asking a model to jump straight from a bug report to a patch often misses multi-step lock interactions, yet letting it reason for thousands of tokens puts every step onto the critical latency path and can exhaust the output limit before any code is emitted. Extending a call along the depth axis lets an autoregressive model unroll intermediate reasoning tokens before emitting its final decision or artifact, generalizing early scratchpad techniques and chain-of-thought prompting [@nye2021show; @wei2022cot]. In the connection-pool scenario, these intermediate tokens might trace thread interleavings step by step: acquiring the pool mutex, checking for leaked socket descriptors, and signaling waiter condition variables. Because autoregressive generation conditions on all prior tokens, later decoding steps can inspect earlier derivations, catch flawed assumptions, and change course before emitting code. That gain comes entirely from running extra forward passes over the growing context rather than changing the network weights.

On the hardware, however, extending a single generation path serializes the work. Because transformer decoding at small batch sizes is memory-bandwidth bound, step latency is set by the time needed to stream all model parameters from high-bandwidth memory into processor caches (principle \ref{pri-vol3-memory-bandwidth-decoding}). Wall-clock generation time therefore scales roughly linearly with the number of generated tokens under a fixed serving setup. A long reasoning trace shows only that the accelerator performed more work, not that the resulting code compiles or runs correctly. The runtime must also leave enough output budget for the final patch: a derivation that hits the token limit mid-thought returns a truncated response, which the invocation contract quarantines like any other incomplete call rather than admitting as a candidate.

### Parallel sampling along the breadth axis {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-breadth-axis}

Drawing a single completion commits the repair to whatever hypothesis the model's first tokens favored, and if that initial framing is wrong, extra depth only elaborates a flawed premise. Sampling along the breadth axis hedges against that commitment by requesting multiple candidate patches from the same source excerpt and task specification using stochastic decoding controls. Conditional on a fixed prompt and independent random seeds, these samples are statistically independent draws from the model's output distribution. Even so, they remain bounded by what the model knows: if the model assigns negligible probability mass to a valid thread-notification pattern, every independent sample can repeat the same missing broadcast. Independent draws can still fail in identical ways.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Temperature, top-$\Glyph{k}$, and nucleus sampling controls are established in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-sampling-controls.
:::

Because parallel candidates do not depend on one another, breadth exposes fine-grained concurrency at modest latency cost. Under memory-bandwidth-bound decoding (principle \ref{pri-vol3-memory-bandwidth-decoding}), a batch of $\CandidatePoolSize$ concurrent candidate streams reads the model weights once per step for all $\CandidatePoolSize$ tokens. Spending an allowance of $\CandidatePoolSize \times \OutputLength$ tokens sequentially along the depth axis multiplies generation latency by roughly $\CandidatePoolSize$. Generating $\CandidatePoolSize$ candidates of length $\OutputLength$ in parallel, by contrast, keeps total generation time close to the duration of the longest candidate, $\max_n \DecodeInterval(\OutputLength_n)$, provided the batch stays memory-bandwidth bound and fits in accelerator memory.

Accelerator memory is where breadth extracts its price. Each active generation stream must maintain its own key-value (KV) cache for the tokens it generates. When the serving system shares prefixes across streams, the $\SequenceLength$-token prompt is stored once in memory, and peak KV cache demand scales as

$$
\BreadthPeakKvCacheMemory \propto \SequenceLength + \sum_{n=1}^{\CandidatePoolSize} \OutputLength_n
$$

Without shared prefix caching, the serving engine stores $\CandidatePoolSize$ copies of the prompt's KV tensors, and memory demand scales as $\CandidatePoolSize \SequenceLength + \sum_n \OutputLength_n$. When total KV cache demand exceeds hardware capacity, the serving engine must split candidates into sequential waves. Once forced into waves, breadth latency degrades from the duration of the single longest candidate toward the sum across waves, while memory thrashing and queueing delays stretch individual token latencies. Whether identical prompt prefixes share physical memory or receive provider billing discounts depends on the serving engine.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Block sharing, which stores a common prompt's KV state once for every candidate that branches from it, is developed in @sec-vol3-kv-cache-cow-prefix-sharing.
:::

Breadth also shifts the burden downstream, because generating a wide pool of candidates pays off only if the runtime can tell which candidate is best. A pool that holds a working patch is useless if the selector cannot identify it. In a study of repeated sampling, @brown2024monkeys showed that the probability that at least one candidate is correct (pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$) kept rising across four orders of magnitude of samples. In contrast, practical selectors such as majority voting and learned reward models (scorers trained to predict whether a candidate is correct, examined in @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-outcome-step-evidence) plateaued after a few hundred samples. Candidate selection is therefore a major consumer of compute and verification budget, not an incidental final step.

### Revising from observations along the feedback axis {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-feedback-axis}

Neither a longer chain of thought nor a wider pool of samples tells the model whether a waiting thread actually receives a condition-variable signal at runtime. The feedback axis supplies that missing evidence by executing a check on a candidate and feeding the resulting observation into the next model request. Instead of relying on frozen weights and a static prompt alone, the repair agent proposes a candidate patch, the runtime runs a bounded test suite, and the next model call receives concrete diagnostics such as a stack trace from a deadlocked worker thread. Those runtime observations narrow the next candidate far more sharply than asking the model to reread the original prompt on its own [@shinn2023reflexion].

Verification checks return structured outcomes: failure, pass, or inconclusive execution (such as a test timeout). A failure trace points to broken assertions or regressions; a passing test confirms that the code satisfies the exercised assertions under the tested conditions; and final acceptance remains a separate policy gate. Running diagnostics is itself an external action that consumes CPU and memory, runs inside a sandbox, and adds wall-clock latency even when used only inside deliberation.

Each feedback round is also one more turn of the horizon $\TurnHorizon$, which ties this axis to horizon compounding (@eq-vol3-horizon-compounding). Unchecked turns compound error as $(1-\PerStepErrorRate)^{\TurnHorizon}$, and the introduction showed (@sec-vol3-intro-horizon-arithmetic) that a check which rejects a bad step and retries it resets that compounding. Feedback is the one axis that places such a check inside every turn, so it can lengthen a deliberation without the unchecked compounding its extra turns would otherwise carry, to the extent that its checks deserve trust (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-verification).

Feedback forces strict serialization because the next revision cannot start until the current check finishes and returns its observation. Context policies that append every prior candidate and diagnostic report also make the input prompt grow from turn to turn. For an initial prompt length $\BasePromptLength$, candidate lengths $\OutputLength_j$, and observation lengths $\lvert \TrajectoryObservation_j\rvert$, an append-only policy yields an input length at turn $\TurnIndex$ of

$$\SequenceLength^{(\TurnIndex)} = \BasePromptLength + \sum_{j=1}^{\TurnIndex-1}(\OutputLength_j + \lvert \TrajectoryObservation_j\rvert)$$

This is the append-only growth that @eq-vol3-trajectory-resend priced across a whole trajectory, now confined to one decision, and it drives up prompt prefill latency, accelerator memory usage, and token billing on every round. Context-compaction methods can summarize earlier attempts or drop stale diagnostic traces, but the allocation policy must budget for the full token volume actually sent to the model API.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Context-compaction methods and their scheduling within the request budget are developed in @sec-vol3-context-engineering-compaction.
:::

### The three axes under one output ceiling {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-common-output-ceiling}

Capping generated tokens at a single number does not cap wall-clock latency, accelerator memory, or input-token billing, because depth, breadth, and feedback turn the same output ceiling into different resource loads. Runtimes therefore track four quantities across the three axes: input and output token counts, critical-path wall-clock latency, peak retained accelerator state, and external information gained. Let $\PrefillTime(\SequenceLength)$ be the time required to ingest an $\SequenceLength$-token prompt, $\PerTokenDecodeTime$ the per-token decoding step time, and $\DecodeInterval(\OutputLength)$ the total generation time for $\OutputLength$ tokens. Let $\FeedbackCheckDuration$ be the duration of the external check in feedback round $\TurnIndex$, which is also the turn index of the trajectory. With $\ExtendedDepthLength$ tokens of extended depth, $\CandidatePoolSize$ breadth candidates executed concurrently, and $\TurnHorizon$ feedback turns, the latency dimension decomposes into three critical paths:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\DepthCriticalPathLatency &\approx \PrefillTime(\SequenceLength) + \ExtendedDepthLength\,\PerTokenDecodeTime,\\
\BreadthCriticalPathLatency &\approx \PrefillTime(\SequenceLength) + \max_{n} \DecodeInterval(\OutputLength_n),\\
\FeedbackCriticalPathLatency &\approx \sum_{t=1}^{\TurnHorizon}\bigl(\PrefillTime(\SequenceLength^{(\TurnIndex)}) + \DecodeInterval(\OutputLength_t) + {\FeedbackCheckDuration}_{\TurnIndex}\bigr).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-vol3-allocation-critical-path}

The critical path for breadth assumes the serving cluster has enough memory and compute capacity to decode all $\CandidatePoolSize$ streams concurrently at an unchanged step time. When capacity saturates, decoding falls back into serialized waves and shifts the critical path toward the sum across candidate streams. The feedback expression, by contrast, grows from two sources: sequential check durations $\FeedbackCheckDuration$ and lengthening prompt prefill times $\PrefillTime(\SequenceLength^{(\TurnIndex)})$ as context accumulates. @Eq-vol3-allocation-critical-path covers only latency; @tbl-vol3-allocation-model sets those critical paths beside the tokens processed, the peak model state retained, and the external information acquired.

| **Axis** | **Tokens processed**                                                                                        | **Critical path**                  | **Peak retained model state**                                                                  | **New information**                      |
|:---------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Depth    | $\SequenceLength + \ExtendedDepthLength$                                                                    | One dependent sequence             | One context of $\SequenceLength + \ExtendedDepthLength$ tokens                                 | None beyond the request and weights      |
| Breadth  | $\SequenceLength + \sum_n \OutputLength_n$ (prompt shared)                                                  | Longest candidate, given capacity  | $\CandidatePoolSize$ contexts, $\SequenceLength + \sum_n \OutputLength_n$ tokens if shared     | Sampling variation over the same request |
| Feedback | $\sum_{t}(\SequenceLength^{(\TurnIndex)} + \OutputLength_t)$, with $\SequenceLength^{(\TurnIndex)}$ growing | Sum of turns, including each check | One active context of $\SequenceLength^{(\TurnHorizon)} + \OutputLength_{\TurnHorizon}$ tokens | Observations from executed checks        |

: **Resource model of the three allocation axes**: Symbolic accounting of processed tokens, critical path, retained model state, and information source. Concurrency and prefix sharing are capacity and implementation assumptions, not properties of the axis. {#tbl-vol3-allocation-model tbl-colwidths="[11,23,22,25,19]"}

Of the three axes, only feedback brings in external information absent from the model weights and prompt. The calculation below evaluates these expressions for the connection-pool repair under a fixed output ceiling of 4,096 tokens, showing how equal output ceilings produce different latencies and token bills.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-allocation-axes
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ COMMON OUTPUT CEILING, DIFFERENT EXECUTION TOPOLOGIES (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-03-matched-budget-axes.
# │ Goal: Separate output ceilings, actual spend, and dependent elapsed time.
# │ Show: Input/output counts, hypothetical bills, and generation/check time.
# │ How: Hold model allowance fixed; stipulate four concurrent breadth streams.
# │      Feedback appends each prior candidate and report; no cache discounts.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import BYTES_INT8, dimensionless, param

class AllocationAxes:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    accel = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    prompt = 4_096  # hypothetical fully serialized initial input tokens
    ceiling = 4_096  # common total generated-token ceiling
    candidates = 4  # breadth concurrency and candidate count
    candidate_tokens = 1_024  # hypothetical generated length per short candidate
    rounds = 3  # hypothetical feedback rounds actually used
    report = 340  # tokens appended per complete observation
    check_time = 1.5 * second  # hypothetical duration per feedback check
    price_in = 3 * USD / 1_000_000  # hypothetical per-input-token price
    price_out = 15 * USD / 1_000_000  # hypothetical per-output-token price

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    weights = model.parameters / param * BYTES_INT8
    token_time = (weights / accel.memory.bandwidth).to(second)
    depth_input = prompt
    depth_output = ceiling
    breadth_input = candidates * prompt
    breadth_output = candidates * candidate_tokens
    feedback_input = rounds * prompt + (candidate_tokens + report) * rounds * (rounds - 1) // 2
    feedback_output = rounds * candidate_tokens
    depth_time = depth_output * token_time
    breadth_time = candidate_tokens * token_time
    feedback_time = rounds * (candidate_tokens * token_time + check_time)
    depth_cost = depth_input * price_in + depth_output * price_out
    breadth_cost = breadth_input * price_in + breadth_output * price_out
    feedback_cost = feedback_input * price_in + feedback_output * price_out
    path_ratio = (depth_time / breadth_time).to(dimensionless).magnitude
    bill_ratio = (breadth_cost / depth_cost).to(dimensionless).magnitude
    breadth_premium = breadth_input - depth_input  # (N - 1) P re-read prompt tokens

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(depth_output == breadth_output == ceiling, "Depth and breadth exhaust ceiling")
    check(feedback_output < ceiling, "Feedback uses less than the output ceiling")
    check(feedback_input == 16_380, "Append-only feedback input accounting")
    check(depth_time > feedback_time > breadth_time, "Scenario critical-path ordering")
    check(breadth_premium == (candidates - 1) * prompt, "Breadth premium is the re-read prompt")
    check(bill_ratio > 1 and path_ratio > 1, "Breadth buys path length with bill")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    prompt_str = fmt_int(prompt)
    ceiling_str = fmt_int(ceiling)
    candidates_str = fmt_int(candidates)
    candidate_tokens_str = fmt_int(candidate_tokens)
    rounds_str = fmt_int(rounds)
    report_str = fmt_int(report)
    check_time_str = fmt_time(check_time, unit="s", precision=1)
    price_in_str = fmt_usd(price_in * 1_000_000, precision=0)
    price_out_str = fmt_usd(price_out * 1_000_000, precision=0)
    depth_input_str = fmt_int(depth_input)
    depth_output_str = fmt_int(depth_output)
    breadth_input_str = fmt_int(breadth_input)
    breadth_output_str = fmt_int(breadth_output)
    feedback_input_str = fmt_int(feedback_input)
    feedback_output_str = fmt_int(feedback_output)
    depth_time_str = fmt_time(depth_time, unit="s", precision=2)
    breadth_time_str = fmt_time(breadth_time, unit="s", precision=2)
    feedback_time_str = fmt_time(feedback_time, unit="s", precision=2)
    depth_cost_str = fmt_usd(depth_cost, precision=5)
    breadth_cost_str = fmt_usd(breadth_cost, precision=5)
    feedback_cost_str = fmt_usd(feedback_cost, precision=5)
    path_mult_str = fmt_multiple(path_ratio, precision=0)
    bill_mult_str = fmt_multiple(bill_ratio, precision=1)
    breadth_premium_str = fmt_int(breadth_premium)
```

::: {#nbk-03-matched-budget-axes .callout-notebook title="One decision, three allocations"}

**Problem**: A repair request starts with `{python} AllocationAxes.prompt_str` input tokens and a common ceiling of `{python} AllocationAxes.ceiling_str` generated tokens. How do depth, breadth, and feedback spend that allowance?

**Variables**: Reuse the illustrative per-token generation time from the preceding example. Breadth has capacity for `{python} AllocationAxes.candidates_str` concurrent streams at that same rate. Each short candidate uses `{python} AllocationAxes.candidate_tokens_str` generated tokens. Feedback uses `{python} AllocationAxes.rounds_str` turns, each followed by a `{python} AllocationAxes.check_time_str` check returning `{python} AllocationAxes.report_str` tokens. Later feedback requests append earlier candidates and reports. Hypothetical prices are `{python} AllocationAxes.price_in_str` per million input tokens and `{python} AllocationAxes.price_out_str` per million output tokens, without cache discounts, so each breadth stream is billed for its own copy of the prompt (unlike the shared-prefix row of @tbl-vol3-allocation-model). Generation times omit prefill, queueing, and transport; the feedback time additionally includes its checks. The bill counts model tokens only, and @tbl-vol3-allocation-tradeoffs tallies each allocation's tokens, time, and bill side by side.

| Allocation |                                 Input tokens |                                 Output tokens |              Generation and included checks |                            Model-token bill |
|:-----------|---------------------------------------------:|----------------------------------------------:|--------------------------------------------:|--------------------------------------------:|
| Depth      |    `{python} AllocationAxes.depth_input_str` |    `{python} AllocationAxes.depth_output_str` |    `{python} AllocationAxes.depth_time_str` |    `{python} AllocationAxes.depth_cost_str` |
| Breadth    |  `{python} AllocationAxes.breadth_input_str` |  `{python} AllocationAxes.breadth_output_str` |  `{python} AllocationAxes.breadth_time_str` |  `{python} AllocationAxes.breadth_cost_str` |
| Feedback   | `{python} AllocationAxes.feedback_input_str` | `{python} AllocationAxes.feedback_output_str` | `{python} AllocationAxes.feedback_time_str` | `{python} AllocationAxes.feedback_cost_str` |
: **Allocation accounting under a common output ceiling**: Equal ceilings produce unequal spend. Allowances omit prefill, queueing, selection, and tool charges. {#tbl-vol3-allocation-tradeoffs}

**Math**: In @tbl-vol3-allocation-tradeoffs, depth generates all `{python} AllocationAxes.ceiling_str` tokens along a single path. Breadth generates `{python} AllocationAxes.candidate_tokens_str` tokens on each of `{python} AllocationAxes.candidates_str` concurrent paths, shortening the critical path by `{python} AllocationAxes.path_mult_str`. However, reading the prompt `{python} AllocationAxes.candidates_str` times across unshared streams adds `{python} AllocationAxes.breadth_premium_str` input tokens, multiplying its billing cost to `{python} AllocationAxes.bill_mult_str` that of depth. Feedback accumulates input context over $\TurnHorizon$ turns according to $\TurnHorizon\,\BasePromptLength + (\OutputLength + \lvert \TrajectoryObservation\rvert)\,\TurnHorizon(\TurnHorizon-1)/2$, reaching `{python} AllocationAxes.feedback_input_str` tokens at $\TurnHorizon =$ `{python} AllocationAxes.rounds_str` because each successive round re-reads all prior candidates and observation reports.

**Systems insight**: Breadth trades money for lower wall-clock latency, and its entire billing premium comes from the $(\CandidatePoolSize-1)\SequenceLength$ re-read prompt tokens. The governing ratio is prompt length relative to generated output: a large repository context makes breadth's input bill grow steeply with both $\CandidatePoolSize$ and $\SequenceLength$, whereas a short prompt or a shared prefix cache removes most of that surcharge. Feedback lands between depth and breadth in both latency and billing while remaining the only axis that acquires new runtime observations. Because this accounting leaves out pass rates, it prices the work rather than the quality of the result.

:::

### Internal budgets and external orchestration {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-latent-vs-scaffold}

When a model service hides its intermediate reasoning tokens behind an API, a runtime that gauges effort from the length of the visible reply understates both token spend and latency. Production systems therefore separate two control surfaces: internal model deliberation and external workflow orchestration. A model service may expose an internal reasoning budget that governs how many intermediate tokens a single call may spend, while the runtime independently controls how many calls to dispatch, which tool checks to run, and what context to pass into subsequent requests. Internal budgets adjust depth inside one call; external orchestration governs breadth across branches, schedules sandboxed checks, and assembles revised prompts. Because commercial APIs often redact intermediate reasoning traces, the runtime must read explicit token-usage headers and termination status codes rather than character counts to enforce quotas and track spend.

### How reasoning models spend output allowances {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-reasoning-models}

A model trained to think in a long internal scratchpad can burn its entire output allowance on intermediate steps and return an empty or truncated final answer. **Reasoning models**\index{Reasoning model!definition} are trained with reinforcement learning on tasks with objective, verifiable outcomes, such as formal mathematics, logic puzzles, and unit-tested codebases. There they learn to generate extended intermediate scratchpads that propose solutions, check steps, and backtrack within a single call [@openai2024o1; @deepseekai2025deepseekr1]. At the serving layer, those intermediate reasoning tokens are ordinary autoregressive output tokens: they consume accelerator compute, fill the KV cache, and incur full output-token charges whether the user interface displays them or hides them behind summary metadata. Because that scratchpad draws from the call's output allowance, services expose a reasoning-budget parameter\index{Reasoning budget} that turns sequential depth from a fixed model habit into a per-request runtime knob. The orchestrator can set that knob by task. No matter how high it is set, however, internal reasoning operates strictly over the supplied prompt and static weights. An extended scratchpad can check arithmetic or trace logic across the prompt, but it cannot observe runtime behavior or tell whether a proposed patch fixes a connection leak without running a test suite.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Reinforcement learning on tasks with verifiable outcomes, the training that produces reasoning models, is developed in @sec-vol3-rlvr.
:::

Because models trained with verifiable rewards spend output allowances differently than instruction-tuned models (models adapted to follow example instructions and responses), token ceilings must be calibrated per model family. When internal reasoning traces remain hidden, the runtime can observe only its own call telemetry and check results, which guide orchestration policy rather than guaranteeing that a candidate is correct. Treating depth as a per-call knob still lets the runtime vary token spend across tasks, raising the practical question of which allocation axis pays off at each level of task difficulty.

::: {#exmp-03-compute-optimal-allocation .callout-example title="Compute-optimal test-time allocation"}

**Scenario**: @snell2024scaling evaluated strategies for spending a fixed test-time compute budget across reasoning benchmarks, comparing sequential revision of a single candidate against parallel breadth sampling and search guided by learned process verifiers (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-verification). The study grouped benchmark problems into difficulty tiers by the base model's single-shot success rate.

**Diagnosis**: On easier problems, sequential revision used the budget most effectively, fixing minor mistakes without the overhead of parallel sampling. On moderately difficult problems, hybrid strategies combining parallel exploration with verifier-guided search reached higher accuracy. On the hardest problems, scaling test-time compute hit diminishing returns across all axes. At matched total FLOPs, a well-chosen test-time allocation let a smaller model beat a model 14 times larger whenever the smaller model had a nonzero base success rate. When base success sat near zero, spending FLOPs on a larger base model beat exhausting tokens on parallel rollouts.

**Systems lesson**: With the supplied prompt held fixed, extra reasoning and sampling can surface capabilities the model already has, but they cannot supply missing runtime facts. Feedback can bring new observations into the next call, though their value still depends on the check's coverage and the model's ability to use them. Runtimes should route budgets by estimated difficulty: spend a small budget or a single call on straightforward tasks, use parallel search and feedback on moderately hard tasks, and escalate near-zero-yield requests to a stronger model or a human operator instead of burning tokens on unguided sampling.

:::

Because a runtime does not know a task's true difficulty in advance, it estimates difficulty with cheap, fast signals before committing a large deliberation budget. Common signals include agreement among two or three short pilot samples, fast static linters, and historical failure rates on similar requests. When pilot samples agree and pass static checks, the runtime keeps the budget small and finishes in one call. When pilot samples disagree or linters flag errors, the scheduler escalates to broader sampling or an edit–test–revise loop, and if the budget ceiling is reached without a verified candidate, it stops and escalates to a human operator. Each routing signal acts as a classifier whose precision and recall should be measured on held-out tasks.

In practice, internal depth and external breadth work together. Each rollout may use enough depth to draft a coherent code patch while the runtime samples several such patches in parallel and filters them through a test harness. Even so, the mix has to fit the system's bottlenecks: slow tests stretch the feedback critical path, and weak tests dull the value of each observation. Those same checks also matter during training, because reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards uses them as a training reward. Any blind spot or false pass that causes a bad selection at test time therefore becomes a loophole that training actively optimizes for on every weight update.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How an acceptance check becomes a training reward, and how its gaps are exploited during training, is developed in @sec-vol3-rlvr-rewards.
:::

::: {#chk-03-compute-allocation-axes .callout-checkpoint title="Choosing an allocation"}

- [ ] **Information**: For the connection-pool repair, which axis can separate a short timeout from a missed notification, and why can the other two not?
- [ ] **Concurrency**: If the service admits only one candidate at a time, how long does the notebook's breadth allocation take to generate, and which allocation then has the shortest path?
- [ ] **Breadth premium**: How many extra input tokens does `{python} AllocationAxes.candidates_str`-way breadth read compared with depth for a `{python} AllocationAxes.prompt_str`-token prompt, and what happens to that premium when the repository context grows eightfold?
- [ ] **Evidence**: If a revised patch passes a targeted test, what additional information determines whether the task may stop?

:::

Choosing how to spend compute across depth, breadth, and feedback determines what candidates enter the pool, but generating a good candidate does not help if the selector picks a plausible broken one instead. The next step is choosing among candidates without spending more on selection than the pool is worth.

## Selecting from a Candidate Pool {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-candidate-diversity}

Sampling eight candidate patches for the connection pool helps nothing if seven of them repeat the same broken timeout workaround and the selector picks one of the seven over the single patch that fixes the notification bug. In a typical pool, one candidate might lengthen an acquisition timeout, another might add exponential retries, and a third might change how the connection-return path wakes waiting threads. The runtime has to decide which proposal, if any, has enough supporting evidence to return, and gathering that evidence consumes time and tokens from the same deliberation budget that produced the pool.

Two questions separate generation from selection: whether the pool holds at least one candidate that solves the task, and whether the selector can pick that candidate without accepting a broken one. A generator can flood the pool with proposals without making selection any easier; conversely, a sharper selector can raise end-to-end reliability without sampling a single extra candidate.

### Useful variation among candidates {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-candidate-variation}

Renaming local variables, reformatting comments, or rewriting a loop can produce eight distinct token sequences that all leave the synchronization bug untouched. Surface variation in token sequences does not guarantee diverse repair hypotheses. In the connection-pool repair, candidates add value only when they test different explanations that downstream checks can tell apart. Changing the thread-notification path vs. lengthening the timeout tests two distinct hypotheses. Generating half a dozen slightly reworded versions of the same timeout bump only wastes verification runs.

This problem is separate from statistical dependence. When the task, prompt, base model, and sampling controls stay fixed, separate draws with independent random seeds are genuinely independent and identically distributed (IID). Even so, if the model puts almost all of its probability mass on timeout edits, independent draws will still fill the pool with variations on that one mistake.

Across a mixed production workload, shared model blind spots matter even more. A model often solves familiar patterns reliably while failing every time on an unfamiliar edge case, so repeated samples on a hard task fail together far more often than the average pass rate across all tasks would suggest. While samples on a single fixed task may be conditionally independent, treating attempts across a mixed workload as draws with one shared pass probability hides that clustering. Feedback-driven revision changes the distribution again: once the runtime feeds test errors into later prompts, each new candidate depends directly on what earlier checks found.

A runtime can encourage broader exploration by raising sampling temperature or prompting the model to try distinct diagnostic angles under the same task constraints. Pushing diversity too hard, however, often produces syntax errors, broken invariants, or nonsensical edits. A diversification method earns its keep only if it raises the task pass rate within a fixed compute and latency budget.

To avoid wasting test runs on near-duplicates, the runtime can prune redundant candidates early by deduplicating on structure and behavior. Abstract syntax tree (AST) normalization strips away surface changes such as variable names and whitespace, and behavioral clustering runs candidates on cheap inputs to group those with identical outputs. Using both steps let a competitive code-generation system narrow tens of thousands of raw model samples down to a handful of distinct submissions [@li2022alphacode]. Each method groups candidates by a bounded equivalence relation, whether normalized syntax or matching outputs on a probe set, and deduplication is sound whenever that relation preserves the property the downstream check tests.

### Choosing a selection rule {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-selection-policies}

Picking the most common patch by majority vote fails whenever the model's favored mistake outnumbers the one candidate that fixes the bug, whereas running the full test suite on every raw sample wastes sandbox time on patches that do not even parse. Runtimes therefore combine three kinds of selection signal, ordered by cost and by the strength of the claim each supports: direct execution checks, answer agreement (consensus voting), and learned ranking.

Direct checks, such as a parser, a type checker, or a test harness, test a candidate deterministically against explicit rules. Each establishes only the property it checks, as the scoped check pipeline of @sec-vol3-foundation-model-scoped-check-pipeline showed, so clean compilation says nothing about whether a race condition is gone. Running candidate code is also an external action that requires sandbox isolation, hard timeouts, and tight permission boundaries.

Answer agreement combines independent reasoning paths by vote. In **self-consistency**\index{Self-consistency!definition}, the runtime samples several reasoning chains, normalizes their final answers, and takes the plurality vote [@wang2022self]. That works well for arithmetic, symbolic logic, or short factual answers, but majority vote still reflects only what the generator produces most often. When a model shares a systematic bias or takes a flawed shortcut, independent samples regularly converge on the same wrong answer. For code repair, voting over raw patches is a poor selector: behavioral agreement inherits the coverage limits of the probe inputs, and a minority patch that actually passes the reproducer should beat a popular patch that fails it.

When deterministic checks cannot cover every requirement, learned rankers and model-based judges supply a heuristic ordering. A learned reward model or a secondary large language model (LLM) judge (a model prompted to grade another model's output) can score explanation clarity, check style guidelines, or rank patches before the runtime spends time on heavy integration tests. Even so, ranking and acceptance answer different questions. Ranking orders candidates from best to worst under a score; acceptance decides whether a candidate meets the task contract. If every candidate in the pool is broken, picking the highest-ranked candidate returns the best-looking failure. Returning a candidate instead of abstaining requires a verifier that produces an objective pass or fail result.

::: {#dfn-vol3-verifier-guided-selection .callout-definition title="Verifier-guided selection"}

***Verifier-guided selection***\index{Verifier-guided selection!definition}\index{Verifier!definition} is a selection policy that returns a candidate only when a **verifier**, a check whose criteria and observations the candidate cannot modify, passes it, and abstains when no candidate passes.

1.  **Significance**: Its success rate is capped by pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$, the chance the pool holds a passing candidate (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-pass-at-k), while the share of its selections that are correct depends on both the verifier's passing-set precision and the selection policy (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-check-precision). The fixed IID first-passing policy developed there preserves passing-set precision; ranking among passing candidates need not. Selection coverage and selected correctness together determine the probability of returning a valid result.
2.  **Distinction**: Voting selects what the generator produces most often and learned ranking selects what a scorer prefers; only a verifier's verdict can justify returning a candidate instead of abstaining.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating the verifier's pass as task acceptance; the verdict covers the checked property, and its false acceptance rate grows in importance as the pool's valid-candidate rate falls.

:::

The hypothetical repair pool in @tbl-vol3-candidate-diversity shows what each check stage can and cannot establish. Here a focused reproducer exercises the known race condition, while full regression suites have not yet run.

| **Candidate** | **Proposed repair**                                | **Observed check result**       | **Supported conclusion**                                  |
|:--------------|:---------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------|
| A             | Increase the timeout                               | Compiles; known failure remains | Structural validity is insufficient                       |
| B             | Retry after the timeout                            | Compiles; known failure remains | Different code can preserve the same defect               |
| C             | Change notification handling with malformed syntax | Parsing fails                   | This artifact cannot proceed to execution testing         |
| D             | Change notification handling with valid syntax     | Compiles; reproducer passes     | Promising repair, with untested behavior still unresolved |

: **Evidence for candidate selection**: A hypothetical repair pool separates the proposed mechanism, the observed result, and the conclusion each check supports. {#tbl-vol3-candidate-diversity tbl-colwidths="[12,25,30,33]"}

A production runtime stages these checks cheapest first, following the cost-ordered cascade of @tbl-verification-layers, so that parsing and AST checks drop malformed candidates before they reach sandboxed tests or an LLM judge. Inside a search, the stage order should come from measured run time and rejection rate rather than guesswork. Running a compiled binary in a warm container might take 5 ms, whereas calling a large LLM judge to grade code quality is a full model call that can take 800 ms and eat into the token budget. Comparing several candidates in a single prompt also scales differently with context length than scoring each candidate on its own. Because checking competes directly with generation for time and tokens, selection has to be budgeted as part of test-time compute.

### Candidate availability under pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$ {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-pass-at-k}

When a runtime fails to return a working patch from a pool of $\IndependentAttemptCount$ samples, the engineer needs to know whether the generator never produced a passing patch or the selector threw a passing patch away. **pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$**\index{Pass at k!definition} separates those two failures by measuring the probability that at least one of $\IndependentAttemptCount$ sampled candidates passes the specified tests [@chen2021evaluating].[^fn-passk-metric-origin]

[^fn-passk-metric-origin]: **Origin of pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$**: The metric was introduced to score program synthesis by functional correctness rather than by textual similarity to a reference [@kulal2019spoc]. Because plugging the observed pass fraction $\PassingSampleCount/\GeneratedSampleCount$ into $1-(1-\PassingSampleCount/\GeneratedSampleCount)^\IndependentAttemptCount$ biases the estimate of what breadth buys, @chen2021evaluating replaced it with the combinatorial estimator derived below. \index{Pass at k!origin}

For a fixed task and fixed generation policy, suppose independent samples each pass the tests with probability $\AttemptPassProbability$. The probability that all $\IndependentAttemptCount$ samples fail is $(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\IndependentAttemptCount$, so

$$
\operatorname{pass@}\IndependentAttemptCount = 1-(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\IndependentAttemptCount.
$$

This expression is conditional on that task and sampling policy. To summarize a workload with different task-level pass probabilities, average the task-level quantities; substituting the workload's average $\AttemptPassProbability$ generally gives a different result. For an adaptive policy that revises its prompt after feedback, evaluate the policy's resulting pools rather than assuming they follow this fixed-distribution formula.

In a benchmark, generate $\GeneratedSampleCount \ge \IndependentAttemptCount$ candidates for a task and let $\PassingSampleCount$ pass the fixed test criterion. Of the $\binom{\GeneratedSampleCount}{\IndependentAttemptCount}$ subsets of size $\IndependentAttemptCount$, exactly $\binom{\GeneratedSampleCount-\PassingSampleCount}{\IndependentAttemptCount}$ contain only failures. The subset estimator is therefore

$$
\PassAtKEstimate
= 1-\frac{\binom{\GeneratedSampleCount-\PassingSampleCount}{\IndependentAttemptCount}}{\binom{\GeneratedSampleCount}{\IndependentAttemptCount}},
$$

with the numerator taken as zero when $\GeneratedSampleCount-\PassingSampleCount<\IndependentAttemptCount$. Under independent, identically distributed sampling for the fixed task, this estimates the probability that a fresh pool of $\IndependentAttemptCount$ candidates contains a test-passing member without bias; @sec-vol3-appendix-math-pass-at-k derives this expectation and details evaluation without factorials. Benchmark results average these estimates over tasks [@chen2021evaluating].

The relationship to deployed selection follows from the event being measured. If the selector must return an unchanged member of the same pool, it cannot return a test-passing candidate when the pool contains none. Its probability of returning a test-passing candidate is therefore at most pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$, counting abstention as no returned pass. A selector that always finds a passing member whenever one exists reaches this ceiling; whether the deployed selector does, within the deployment's checking budget, is a separate measurement.

The predicate in pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$ is passing these tests, which is narrower than satisfying the complete task requirements. The ceiling also covers only selectors that return an unchanged pool member rather than repairing candidates or synthesizing a new artifact. Benchmarks therefore report candidate availability alongside selected-output performance under the relevant criterion, because the gap between the two can be large. @Fig-vol3-coverage-vs-selection recomputes the plateau described in @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-breadth-axis from the released per-sample correctness labels of @brown2024monkeys. It plots coverage (the task-averaged pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$ estimate) against the accuracy of majority voting over the same pools.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-coverage-vs-selection
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ COVERAGE VS. SELECTED ACCURACY (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-vol3-coverage-vs-selection and the paragraph after it.
# │ Goal: Quantify the gap between pool availability and what a voting
# │       selector returns.
# │ Show: Coverage and majority-vote accuracy at the largest pool; the
# │       vote's gain after 256 samples; repository-repair coverage growth.
# │ How:  Literature.RepeatedSamplingMajority / RepeatedSamplingCoverage,
# │       recomputed from per-sample labels with the unbiased estimator.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Literature
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_percent

def _at(rows, model, dataset, k, field):
    return next(r[field] for r in rows if r["model"] == model and r["dataset"] == dataset and r["k"] == k)

class CoverageVsSelection:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    maj = Literature.RepeatedSamplingMajority.entries
    cov = Literature.RepeatedSamplingCoverage.entries
    small, large = "Llama-3-8B-Instruct", "Llama-3-70B-Instruct"
    k_max, k_knee = 10_000, 256
    repair = "DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct + Moatless Tools"
    repair_set, repair_k = "SWE-bench Lite (all 300)", 250

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    cov_small = _at(maj, small, "MATH", k_max, "coverage")
    vote_small = _at(maj, small, "MATH", k_max, "majority_vote_accuracy")
    vote_large = _at(maj, large, "MATH", k_max, "majority_vote_accuracy")
    vote_gain_after_knee = 0.0
    for _m in (small, large):
        vote_gain_after_knee = max(
            vote_gain_after_knee, _at(maj, _m, "MATH", k_max, "majority_vote_accuracy") - _at(maj, _m, "MATH", k_knee, "majority_vote_accuracy")
        )
    cov_gain_after_knee = cov_small - _at(maj, small, "MATH", k_knee, "coverage")
    repair_1 = _at(cov, repair, repair_set, 1, "coverage")
    repair_k_cov = _at(cov, repair, repair_set, repair_k, "coverage")

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    check(cov_small > 0.95 and vote_small < 0.5 and vote_large < 0.65, "Prose contrasts near-complete coverage with sub-60% voting")
    check(vote_gain_after_knee < 0.01 < 0.05 < cov_gain_after_knee, "Prose says voting stalls after 256 samples while coverage keeps rising")
    check(repair_k_cov > 3 * repair_1, "Prose says repository-repair coverage more than triples")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    k_max_str, k_knee_str, repair_k_str = fmt_int(k_max), fmt_int(k_knee), fmt_int(repair_k)
    cov_small_str = fmt_percent(round(cov_small, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    vote_small_str = fmt_percent(round(vote_small, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    vote_large_str = fmt_percent(round(vote_large, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    cov_gain_str = fmt_int(round(100 * cov_gain_after_knee))
    repair_1_str = fmt_percent(round(repair_1, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    repair_cov_str = fmt_percent(round(repair_k_cov, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
```

:::: {#fig-vol3-coverage-vs-selection fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Availability Outruns Selection**: Coverage (solid), the share of problems whose pool holds a correct candidate, and majority-vote accuracy (dashed) on competition mathematics for two model sizes, against pool size on a logarithmic axis; the dotted line is coverage for a repository-repair agent whose candidates are checked by tests. Coverage keeps climbing for four orders of magnitude while voting flattens after a few hundred samples, so most of the candidates a large pool adds are correct answers the voting selector never returns. Recomputed from the per-sample labels released by @brown2024monkeys." fig-alt="Line chart of percent of problems from 0 to 100 against samples per problem from 1 to 10,000 on a logarithmic axis. At `{python} CoverageVsSelection.k_max_str` samples, the smaller model's pools hold a correct answer for `{python} CoverageVsSelection.cov_small_str` of the problems, yet majority voting returns one for `{python} CoverageVsSelection.vote_small_str`, and `{python} CoverageVsSelection.vote_large_str` for the larger model. Beyond `{python} CoverageVsSelection.k_knee_str` samples the vote gains less than a point while coverage gains another `{python} CoverageVsSelection.cov_gain_str`. The repair agent's coverage rises from `{python} CoverageVsSelection.repair_1_str` with one sample to `{python} CoverageVsSelection.repair_cov_str` at `{python} CoverageVsSelection.repair_k_str`, but that growth is usable only because tests can identify which candidate passes. Spending on breadth is therefore justified by the selector, not by the pool. Without a check that recognizes the correct candidate, the added samples raise the pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$ ceiling without raising what the runtime returns.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The distinction between pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$ over a candidate pool and consistency over repeated system runs is developed in @sec-vol3-evaluation-pass-k.
:::

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_ttc_margin_pass_at_n.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Four horizontal green bars for candidate pools, from top: 8, 4, 2, and 1 candidates, labeled 94, 76, 51, and 30 percent."}

*Each doubling squares the chance that all candidates fail, so the bars approach certainty.*
:::

Breadth has a price that pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$ makes easy to compute. In **best-of-$\CandidatePoolSize$ sampling**\index{Best-of-N sampling!definition}, the runtime generates $\CandidatePoolSize$ candidates for one decision and returns one that its selector admits. The pool is the same object pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$ describes, so its availability is pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$ with $\IndependentAttemptCount = \CandidatePoolSize$, written pass@$\CandidatePoolSize$ from here on. The notebook below prices that pool against the simplest alternative, generating one candidate at a time and stopping at the first pass, under the most favorable selection assumption, in which the verifier is the acceptance check itself.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-best-of-n-price
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE PRICE OF A LARGER POOL (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-03-best-of-n-pool-price; fallacies (mixed-workload pass@N).
# │ Goal: Compare parallel best-of-N with stop-at-first-pass sequential retry
# │       at the same success probability.
# │ Show: pass@N, marginal gain of the last candidate, candidates per success.
# │ How: IID candidates for a fixed task; the verifier is the acceptance check;
# │      a perfect selector returns a passing member whenever one exists.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

class BestOfN:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    p = 0.30  # hypothetical per-candidate pass probability for a fixed task
    pools = (1, 2, 4, 8)  # pool sizes compared
    p_easy = 0.60  # hypothetical mixed workload: half the tasks pass at this rate
    p_hard = 0.0  # hypothetical mixed workload: the other half never pass

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_max = pools[-1]
    pass_at = []
    for n in pools:
        pass_at.append(1 - (1 - p) ** n)
    pass_max = pass_at[-1]
    last_gain = p * (1 - p) ** (n_max - 1)
    parallel_per_success = n_max / pass_max
    seq_candidates = pass_max / p  # expected attempts, stop at first pass, cap n_max
    seq_per_success = seq_candidates / pass_max  # reduces to 1 / p
    cost_ratio = parallel_per_success / seq_per_success
    p_mix = (p_easy + p_hard) / 2
    naive_mix = 1 - (1 - p_mix) ** n_max
    true_mix = ((1 - (1 - p_easy) ** n_max) + (1 - (1 - p_hard) ** n_max)) / 2

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(pass_at == sorted(set(pass_at)), "pass@N rises with N")
    check(abs(seq_per_success - 1 / p) < 1e-12, "Sequential retry costs 1/p per success")
    check(cost_ratio > 2, "Parallel pool costs over twice as much per success")
    check(abs(p_mix - p) < 1e-12, "Mixed workload has the same average rate")
    check(true_mix < naive_mix - 0.3, "Averaging p overstates mixed-workload pass@N")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    p_str = fmt_percent(p, precision=0, style="prose")
    n_max_str = fmt_int(n_max)
    pools_str = MarkdownStr(", ".join(str(n) for n in pools[:-1]) + ", and " + str(pools[-1]))
    pass_1_str = fmt_int(round(100 * pass_at[0]))
    pass_2_str = fmt_int(round(100 * pass_at[1]))
    pass_4_str = fmt_int(round(100 * pass_at[2]))
    pass_max_str = fmt_percent(pass_max, precision=1, style="prose")
    last_gain_pts_str = fmt(last_gain * 100, precision=1)
    parallel_per_success_str = fmt(parallel_per_success, precision=1)
    seq_candidates_str = fmt(seq_candidates, precision=2)
    seq_per_success_str = fmt(seq_per_success, precision=1)
    cost_mult_str = fmt_multiple(cost_ratio, precision=1)
    p_easy_str = fmt_percent(p_easy, precision=0, style="prose")
    naive_mix_str = fmt_percent(naive_mix, precision=1, style="prose")
    true_mix_str = fmt_percent(true_mix, precision=1, style="prose")
```

::: {#nbk-03-best-of-n-pool-price .callout-notebook title="The price of a larger pool"}

**Problem**: Each candidate repair passes the task's verifier with probability $\AttemptPassProbability$, independently for this task, and the verifier is the acceptance check. How many candidates per accepted repair does a parallel pool of $\CandidatePoolSize$ spend, compared with sequential retry that stops at the first pass and gives up after $\CandidatePoolSize$ attempts?

**Variables**: $\AttemptPassProbability$ = `{python} BestOfN.p_str` (hypothetical); pools of `{python} BestOfN.pools_str` candidates; a selector that returns a passing member whenever one exists.

**Math**: The formula pass@$\CandidatePoolSize = 1-(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\CandidatePoolSize$ gives `{python} BestOfN.pass_1_str`, `{python} BestOfN.pass_2_str`, `{python} BestOfN.pass_4_str`, and `{python} BestOfN.pass_max_str` for those pools. The last of `{python} BestOfN.n_max_str` candidates adds $\AttemptPassProbability(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^{\CandidatePoolSize-1}$, only `{python} BestOfN.last_gain_pts_str` percentage points. The parallel pool always spends `{python} BestOfN.n_max_str` candidates, or `{python} BestOfN.parallel_per_success_str` per accepted repair. Sequential retry fails only when all `{python} BestOfN.n_max_str` attempts fail, so it reaches the same `{python} BestOfN.pass_max_str`, yet it spends on average $[1-(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\CandidatePoolSize]/\AttemptPassProbability$ = `{python} BestOfN.seq_candidates_str` candidates, or $1/\AttemptPassProbability$ = `{python} BestOfN.seq_per_success_str` per accepted repair.

**Systems insight**: At equal success, the parallel pool costs `{python} BestOfN.cost_mult_str` as much per accepted repair; what it buys is one round instead of an expected `{python} BestOfN.seq_candidates_str` sequential generate-and-check rounds. Breadth buys latency, not cost. In $\CostPerAcceptedTask = \mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]/\AcceptanceProbability$ it raises $\AcceptanceProbability$ per round but raises the attempt cost faster. Size $\CandidatePoolSize$ as the smallest pool whose pass@$\CandidatePoolSize$ meets the target within the rounds the deadline allows, and stop growing it once the next candidate's gain is worth less than its cost.

:::

### Balancing pool size against checking cost {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-selection-costs}

Growing the candidate pool raises the chance that a valid repair enters the pool, but it also multiplies the checking load. Under a fixed deliberation budget, spending nearly everything on generation starves verification and forces the selector onto cheap, shallow heuristics. A smaller pool paired with a thorough check often beats a large pool paired with a weak selector; only when candidate generation itself is the bottleneck does a wider pool pay off right away. Comparing the two regimes therefore requires pricing generation and selection together rather than tuning either stage on its own.

Checker errors also compound as the pool grows, because each extra invalid candidate gives an imperfect verifier another chance to register a false pass. If a verifier has a 5 percent false acceptance rate (it passes 5 percent of invalid candidates, defined formally in @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-check-precision), testing twenty invalid candidates with independent check outcomes makes at least one false pass more likely than not ($1 - (1 - 0.05)^{20} \approx 64\%$). Whether the selector actually returns that false pass depends on what else sits in the pool and on the tie-breaking rule, a distinction the next section makes exact. The defect rate of the returned candidate depends on the generator's base rate of valid candidates, the check's false-acceptance and false-rejection rates, and how the selector chooses among passing candidates. When an adaptive search steers generation using verifier scores, it shifts all three quantities at once and can push candidates straight into the verifier's blind spots.

Where the runtime checks candidates along the trajectory sets both selection latency and cost. Checking only completed candidates works well when end-to-end tests are fast and decisive, whereas checking intermediate steps lets the runtime prune broken branches before spending tokens on their completions. That trade-off separates outcome checks, which test finished artifacts, from process checks, which score intermediate steps.

## Verifying Candidates {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-verification}

In a connection-pool repair, clean compilation confirms only syntax and types, and even a targeted concurrency test exercises only a handful of thread schedules and can miss a race condition. Every verification check answers a bounded question, never the whole question of whether a candidate is safe to ship. Engineers therefore have to decide which checks to run, whether to attach them to finished candidates or to intermediate steps, and how much trust to place in a passing verdict when valid candidates are rare.

### Checking whole outputs vs. intermediate steps {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-outcome-step-evidence}

Waiting until a candidate patch is completely written before running any check wastes every token spent elaborating a diagnosis that went wrong in step one, whereas scoring every intermediate step from scratch rescans the growing prefix again and again. An **outcome check**\index{Outcome check!definition} tests a completed candidate against an external rule, such as whether a patched service passes an end-to-end regression suite. An **outcome reward model**\index{Outcome reward model!definition}, by contrast, predicts a scalar quality score for the finished candidate, like the learned verifiers trained to rank candidate solutions in mathematical reasoning [@cobbe2021training]. The outcome check runs the artifact and reports what happened; the reward model only predicts how good the artifact looks.

Step-level checks evaluate intermediate claims or partial states before the candidate is complete. In the connection-pool repair, a step check can test whether a waiting worker receives a wake-up signal before the agent drafts a full timeout patch. If the trace refutes the timeout explanation, the runtime drops that branch immediately and saves the remaining generation tokens. Learned process scorers similarly score or prune partial reasoning traces, using low step scores as early warnings of downstream failure. **Process supervision**\index{Process supervision!definition}[^fn-prm-step-labels] attaches feedback to discrete intermediate steps rather than waiting for the final answer [@uesato2022solving; @lightman2023let]. What separates outcome feedback from process feedback is where the signal attaches, not what the scorer reads, since a learned outcome scorer can also read the full reasoning trace before grading the final output.

[^fn-prm-step-labels]: **Step-Level Labels (PRM800K)**: Outcome labels for code can be produced automatically by running tests. Step labels require a judgment on each intermediate step, and the PRM800K dataset used to train the process reward model of @lightman2023let contains about 800,000 human step-level labels.
