That labeling cost is one reason learned process scorers are scarcer than outcome checks. \index{Process reward model!labeling cost}

::: {#dfn-process-reward-model .callout-definition title="Process reward model (PRM)"}

A ***process reward model*** (PRM)\index{Process reward model!definition} is a learned scorer that assigns a value to each intermediate step of a candidate trajectory, conditioned on the task context and the preceding steps.

1.  **Significance**: Step scores allow search algorithms to prune unpromising branches early, keeping beam search and tree search, the search procedures that extend only the best-scoring partial candidates (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-search-structures), within finite computational budgets.
2.  **Distinction**: An outcome reward model evaluates only terminal states; a process reward model assigns credit across intermediate steps. This early steering capability requires dense step-level supervision, which costs substantially more to gather than automated test outcomes.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Mistaking a high step score for verified correctness. A process reward model provides heuristic guidance for ranking and pruning, but it offers no formal guarantees and satisfies no closure evidence level.

:::

Each granularity catches failures the other misses. An outcome check tests the assembled artifact end to end, catching integration bugs that look harmless inside any single step. A process check catches errors early and stops broken branches from burning more generation tokens, but checking too often adds scorer overhead and risks pruning good branches when step scores are noisy. Choosing how often to check balances saved generation tokens against scorer cost and false rejections.

Step-scoring cost also depends on whether the serving engine reuses prefix state across steps. Suppose a scorer reads a task prompt of $\SequenceLength$ tokens plus the candidate's growing prefix after each of its $\ScoredStepCount$ steps, where each step adds $\FiniteChange \ScoredPrefixLength$ tokens. Scoring each cumulative prefix from scratch, without reusing key-value cache state from earlier steps, processes

$$
\sum_{j=1}^{\ScoredStepCount}\left(\SequenceLength + \ScoredStepIndex\,\FiniteChange \ScoredPrefixLength\right) = \ScoredStepCount \SequenceLength + \frac{\ScoredStepCount(\ScoredStepCount+1)}{2}\,\FiniteChange \ScoredPrefixLength
$$ {#eq-vol3-prm-rescoring}

scorer input tokens, which grows quadratically with the number of steps $\ScoredStepCount$. The beam-search calculation later in this chapter (notebook \ref{nbk-03-compute-allocation-and-latency-trade-offs}) charges the $\ScoredStepIndex\,\FiniteChange \ScoredPrefixLength$ term of @eq-vol3-prm-rescoring, with the task prompt $\SequenceLength$ excluded, for every extension scored at step $\ScoredStepIndex$. When the serving engine caches prefixes across steps, incremental scoring reads only the new $\FiniteChange \ScoredPrefixLength$ tokens at each step and removes the quadratic growth; scorers that must re-read the whole candidate without prefix caching pay the full sum.

@Tbl-vol3-verifier-classes compares four common kinds of check by what they inspect, where they can be fooled, whether they are deterministic, and which closure evidence level (@sec-vol3-intro-invariant-closure) they reach. Compilers and sealed test suites establish bounded, reproducible facts within their scope, whereas learned scorers only rank or prune candidates.

| **Check**                | **Evaluates**                      | **Coverage**                              | **False-acceptance exposure**                    | **Deterministic**           | **Closure evidence level**                              |
|:-------------------------|:-----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|
| Outcome scorer (learned) | Completed candidate                | Any representation it was trained to read | Persuasive but wrong final text                  | No                          | None; ranks only                                        |
| Process scorer (learned) | Intermediate step given its prefix | Steps it can delimit and judge            | Locally plausible steps that drift from the task | No                          | None; ranks and prunes only                             |
| Compiler or type checker | Syntax and declared types          | Properties expressible in the type system | Behavior outside the type system                 | Yes                         | Static analysis                                         |
| Sealed test suite        | Behavior on withheld cases         | The cases and schedules it exercises      | Untested inputs and schedules                    | Yes, under fixed conditions | Sealed tests, if the candidate cannot read or modify it |

: **Kinds of check and the claims they support**: Learned scorers order candidates; compilers and sealed suites establish bounded properties. None dominates the others on every task, and a deterministic verdict remains incomplete outside its coverage. {#tbl-vol3-verifier-classes tbl-colwidths="[17,17,18,20,11,17]"}

### How base rates limit check precision {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-check-precision}

When only 5 percent of generated patches actually fix a bug, even a test suite that falsely passes just 2 percent of broken patches leaves nearly a third of all passing candidates defective. The reliability question for any check is what share of the candidates that pass it are genuinely valid. Call meeting the full task specification $\text{Valid}$ and receiving a positive check verdict $\text{PASS}$. Let $\ValidCandidateRate = \Pr(\text{Valid})$ be the base rate of valid candidates in the generator's output distribution, $\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate = \Pr(\text{PASS}\mid\neg\text{Valid})$ the **false acceptance rate**\index{False acceptance rate!definition}, and $\VerifierFalseRejectionRate = \Pr(\neg\text{PASS}\mid\text{Valid})$ the **false rejection rate**\index{False rejection rate!definition}. Here "acceptance" means passing the internal verifier, not authorization to ship to production. The valid-candidate rate $\ValidCandidateRate$ is not the test-pass probability $\AttemptPassProbability$ used in pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$: $\ValidCandidateRate$ is the chance of meeting the full task specification, whereas $\AttemptPassProbability$ is the chance of passing the stated tests. A perfect check makes the two coincide; an imperfect check separates them, and the precision formula below measures the gap.

The total probability that a random candidate passes the verifier is $\VerifierPassProbability=\ValidCandidateRate(1-\VerifierFalseRejectionRate)+(1-\ValidCandidateRate)\,\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate$. Applying the same Bayes' rule that gave the defect share among one checker's passing patches (@eq-vol3-fm-checker-posterior) gives the precision of positive verdicts:

$$
\VerifierPrecision \equiv \Pr(\text{Valid}\mid\text{PASS})
=\frac{\ValidCandidateRate(1-\VerifierFalseRejectionRate)}{\ValidCandidateRate(1-\VerifierFalseRejectionRate)+(1-\ValidCandidateRate)\,\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate}.
$$ {#eq-vol3-verifier-precision}

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_ttc_margin_precision_base_rate.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="A dark curve of the valid share among passing candidates plotted against the valid-candidate rate. It rises steeply at low rates and flattens near the top. The low-rate region is shaded red, and a red dot is labeled 5 percent valid, 70 percent of passes."}

*At a low valid rate, even a strict check passes many invalid candidates.*
:::

When valid candidates are rare, even a check with a small false acceptance rate produces a passing pool where broken candidates make up a large share, the same base-rate trap that @sec-vol3-foundation-model-self-review-evidence showed for a single checked patch. Applied across a candidate pool, this is the verification asymmetry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}) in quantitative form. Generating a passing candidate and knowing that a passing candidate is valid are different events, and the base rate and checker error rates, not the pool size, bound how far a pass can be trusted. Both error rates therefore have to be measured on real tasks for each model family and test harness.

While @eq-vol3-verifier-precision describes the pool of passing candidates as a whole, the reliability of the single candidate the runtime *returns* depends on the selection rule. Suppose candidate-check pairs are drawn independently and identically for a fixed task under constant error rates. Suppose also that the runtime checks the pool in a fixed order unrelated to quality, returns the first candidate that passes, and abstains if none passes. Under that first-passing rule, the probability that a returned candidate is valid equals $\VerifierPrecision$: learning that earlier candidates in the list failed does not change the conditional validity of the first one that passes. Picking the candidate with the highest continuous reward score behaves differently, because maximizing a noisy score actively concentrates positive scoring errors, as the next subsection shows.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: compute-vol3-ttc-check-yield
# ┌── LEGO ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-03-compute-overhead-and-yield-under
# │ Goal: Separate passing-set precision, selection coverage, and incident loss.
# │ Show: A hypothetical fixed-batch first-pass selection policy.
# │ How: IID candidate/check outcomes, fixed rates, abstention if none passes.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check
import math
from mlsysim.core.units import dimensionless

class CheckYield:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────
    n = 64
    tokens_per_candidate = 1_024 * token
    output_price = 15 * USD / Mtoken
    p = 0.05
    eps_fr = 0.10  # false rejection rate, epsilon_FR (hypothetical)
    eps_fa = 0.02  # false acceptance rate, epsilon_FA (hypothetical)
    incident_loss = 500 * USD

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Physics & Logic) ─────────────────────────────────────────
    valid_pass = p * (1 - eps_fr)
    invalid_pass = (1 - p) * eps_fa
    pass_probability = valid_pass + invalid_pass
    precision = valid_pass / pass_probability
    defect_given_selection = 1 - precision
    any_selection = 1 - (1 - pass_probability) ** n
    no_selection = 1 - any_selection
    wrong_selection = any_selection * defect_given_selection
    any_false_pass = 1 - (1 - invalid_pass) ** n
    expected_valid_passes = n * valid_pass
    expected_invalid_passes = n * invalid_pass
    expected_passes = n * pass_probability
    conditional_loss = defect_given_selection * incident_loss
    task_loss = wrong_selection * incident_loss
    output_bill = (n * tokens_per_candidate * output_price).to(USD)
    # Sensitivity: halve the false acceptance rate, or double the valid rate.
    precision_half_fa = valid_pass / (valid_pass + (1 - p) * eps_fa / 2)
    precision_double_p = 2 * p * (1 - eps_fr) / (2 * p * (1 - eps_fr) + (1 - 2 * p) * eps_fa)
    loss_to_bill = (task_loss / output_bill).to(dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(pass_probability > 0, "Passing-set precision requires q > 0.")
    check(isinstance(n, int) and n > 0, "n must be a positive int")
    check(all(0 <= rate <= 1 for rate in (p, eps_fa, eps_fr)), "rates must be in [0, 1]")
    check(
        all(
            0 <= probability <= 1
            for probability in (
                valid_pass,
                invalid_pass,
                pass_probability,
                precision,
                defect_given_selection,
                any_selection,
                no_selection,
                wrong_selection,
                any_false_pass,
            )
        ),
        "probabilities must be in [0, 1]",
    )
    check(math.isclose(precision + defect_given_selection, 1), "precision + defect must sum to 1")
    check(math.isclose(any_selection + no_selection, 1), "any + no selection must sum to 1")
    check(0 <= expected_valid_passes <= n, "expected valid passes in bounds")
    check(0 <= expected_invalid_passes <= n, "expected invalid passes in bounds")
    check(0 <= expected_passes <= n, "expected passes in bounds")
    check(math.isclose(expected_valid_passes + expected_invalid_passes, expected_passes), "expected passes must sum")
    check(wrong_selection <= any_selection, "wrong selection <= any selection")
    check(wrong_selection <= any_false_pass, "wrong selection <= any false pass")
    check(math.isclose(wrong_selection, any_selection * defect_given_selection), "wrong selection identity")
    check(tokens_per_candidate > 0 * token, "tokens per candidate must be positive")
    check(output_price >= 0 * USD / Mtoken, "output price non-negative")
    check(output_bill >= 0 * USD, "output bill non-negative")
    check(0 * USD <= task_loss <= conditional_loss <= incident_loss, "loss hierarchy must hold")
    check(math.isclose(task_loss.to(USD).magnitude, (any_selection * conditional_loss).to(USD).magnitude), "task loss identity")
    check(precision < precision_half_fa < 1 and precision < precision_double_p < 1, "sensitivity ordering")
    check(loss_to_bill > 100, "loss to bill ratio > 100")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Human-Readable Outputs) ───────────────────────────────────
    n_str = fmt_int(n)
    tokens_str = fmt_tokens(tokens_per_candidate)
    price_str = fmt_usd(output_price * Mtoken)
    p_str = fmt_percent(p, style="prose")
    eps_fr_str = fmt_percent(eps_fr, style="prose")
    eps_fa_str = fmt_percent(eps_fa, style="prose")
    loss_str = fmt_usd(incident_loss)
    valid_passes_str = fmt(expected_valid_passes, precision=2)
    invalid_passes_str = fmt(expected_invalid_passes, precision=3)
    passes_str = fmt(expected_passes, precision=3)
    precision_str = fmt_percent(precision, precision=2, style="prose")
    defect_str = fmt_percent(defect_given_selection, precision=2, style="prose")
    coverage_str = fmt_percent(any_selection, precision=2, style="prose")
    abstention_str = fmt_percent(no_selection, precision=2, style="prose")
    wrong_str = fmt_percent(wrong_selection, precision=2, style="prose")
    any_false_str = fmt_percent(any_false_pass, precision=2, style="prose")
    conditional_loss_str = fmt_usd(conditional_loss, precision=2)
    task_loss_str = fmt_usd(task_loss, precision=2)
    bill_str = fmt_usd(output_bill, precision=2)
    precision_half_fa_str = fmt_percent(precision_half_fa, precision=1, style="prose")
    precision_double_p_str = fmt_percent(precision_double_p, precision=1, style="prose")
    loss_to_bill_str = fmt_int(round(loss_to_bill))
```

::: {#nbk-03-compute-overhead-and-yield-under .callout-notebook title="Yield and risk under asymmetric verifier error"}

**Problem**: A repair policy generates all `{python} CheckYield.n_str` candidates before selection. It uses the first-passing rule above and abstains when no candidate passes. What does additional breadth buy, and what risk remains?

**Variables**: All rates are hypothetical. Each candidate contains `{python} CheckYield.tokens_str` tokens, billed at `{python} CheckYield.price_str` per million output tokens. The valid-candidate rate is `{python} CheckYield.p_str`, false rejection is `{python} CheckYield.eps_fr_str`, and false acceptance is `{python} CheckYield.eps_fa_str`. Suppose a separately authorized deployment policy deploys the selected candidate without further checking. A defective deployment incurs `{python} CheckYield.loss_str` in incident loss. For this calculation alone, valid deployments and abstentions incur zero incident loss, and missed repairs and delay are left unpriced.

**Math**: The expected passing counts are `{python} CheckYield.valid_passes_str` valid candidates and `{python} CheckYield.invalid_passes_str` invalid candidates, totaling `{python} CheckYield.passes_str`. @Eq-vol3-verifier-precision yields `{python} CheckYield.precision_str` precision. Conditional on making a selection, the probability of a defective selection is therefore `{python} CheckYield.defect_str`, with expected incident loss `{python} CheckYield.conditional_loss_str` per selected deployment.

The probability of any selection is $1-(1-\VerifierPassProbability)^\CandidatePoolSize$, or `{python} CheckYield.coverage_str`; the policy abstains on `{python} CheckYield.abstention_str` of batches. Multiplying selection coverage by conditional defect probability gives `{python} CheckYield.wrong_str` defective selections per task attempt and `{python} CheckYield.task_loss_str` expected incident loss per attempt, including abstentions. Generating the entire batch costs `{python} CheckYield.bill_str` in output charges. Input charges, checking, and other operational costs are omitted. A sequential policy that stops generation at the first pass would have a different generation bill.

**Systems insight**: Expected incident loss per attempt is about `{python} CheckYield.loss_to_bill_str` times the output bill, so the acceptance policy, not the token price, sets the cost of this task. Precision responds to two knobs of similar strength: halving the false acceptance rate raises it from `{python} CheckYield.precision_str` to `{python} CheckYield.precision_half_fa_str`, and doubling the valid-candidate rate raises it to `{python} CheckYield.precision_double_p_str`. More candidates move neither. At a low base rate, spend on whichever of a better generator or a stricter check is cheaper, and price false rejections too when a missed valid repair is costly.

:::

With $\ValidCandidateRate$, $\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate$, and $\VerifierFalseRejectionRate$ held fixed, growing the pool size $\CandidatePoolSize$ does not change precision $\VerifierPrecision$. A wider pool raises the chance of finding at least one passing candidate, but it also raises the chance that the batch holds at least one false pass: $1-[1-(1-\ValidCandidateRate)\,\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate]^\CandidatePoolSize$. In the calculation above, that false-pass exposure reaches `{python} CheckYield.any_false_str`, while the probability of actually returning a defective candidate is `{python} CheckYield.wrong_str`. The gap arises because under a first-passing rule a false pass later in the batch does no harm if an earlier valid candidate passes first. Pool availability, passing-set precision, and deployed defect risk are three distinct numbers.

### How search exploits imperfect checks {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-selection-pressure}

The more candidates a search generates and ranks against an imperfect scorer or test suite, the more likely the winning candidate is one that exploited a scorer blind spot or deleted a failing assertion rather than fixing the bug. Fixed error rates describe passive sampling from a fixed distribution, but adaptive search changes the candidates themselves. When a search policy steers generation or picks the maximum of a noisy score, it pushes candidates into regions where the evaluator is poorly calibrated, so the baseline rates $\ValidCandidateRate$, $\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate$, and $\VerifierFalseRejectionRate$ no longer hold for the candidates that reach the end of the search. Optimizing against an imperfect proxy breaks down in three distinct ways [@manheim2018categorizing]. Manheim and Garrabrant classify them as forms of Goodhart's law.[^fn-goodhart-law-origin] In *regressional* Goodhart, picking the highest score selects for positive measurement noise. In *extremal* Goodhart, correlations that hold on typical candidates break down in the tail reached by search. In *adversarial* Goodhart, candidate code tampers with or bypasses the test harness.

[^fn-goodhart-law-origin]: **Goodhart's Law**: The economist Charles Goodhart stated it in 1975 about monetary policy: any observed statistical regularity tends to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes [@goodhart1984]. The anthropologist Marilyn Strathern later gave it the form usually quoted today, that when a measure becomes a target it ceases to be a good measure [@strathern1997improving]. A test suite used to select patches is such a regularity, a reliable description of past candidates that weakens once search optimizes against it. \index{Goodhart's law!origin}

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-argmax-selection
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SELECTION ON A NOISY SCORE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-selection-pressure.
# │ Goal: Show how argmax selection concentrates positive scoring error, and
# │       how a rare checker gap becomes likely in a large pool.
# │ Show: Exact expected maximum of N standard normal errors; exploit presence.
# │ How: Numerical integration of N x phi(x) Phi(x)^(N-1); IID candidates.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
import math

def expected_max_std_normal(n, lo=-10.0, hi=10.0, steps=40_000):
    """Trapezoidal integral of x * n * phi(x) * Phi(x)**(n - 1)."""
    dx = (hi - lo) / steps
    total = 0.0
    for i in range(steps + 1):
        x = lo + i * dx
        pdf = math.exp(-0.5 * x * x) / math.sqrt(2 * math.pi)
        cdf = 0.5 * (1 + math.erf(x / math.sqrt(2)))
        weight = 0.5 if i in (0, steps) else 1.0
        total += weight * x * n * pdf * cdf ** (n - 1)
    return total * dx

class ArgmaxSelection:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    n_small = 4  # hypothetical small pool
    n_large = 64  # same batch size as the yield notebook
    gap_rate = 0.005  # hypothetical fraction of candidates exploiting a check gap

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    shift_small = expected_max_std_normal(n_small)
    shift_large = expected_max_std_normal(n_large)
    asym_large = math.sqrt(2 * math.log(n_large))
    gap_present = 1 - (1 - gap_rate) ** n_large

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(expected_max_std_normal(1)) < 1e-6, "Mean of one standard normal is zero")
    check(0 < shift_small < shift_large < asym_large, "Selected error grows with N, below the asymptote")
    check(0 < gap_present < 1, "Probability bounds")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    n_small_str = fmt_int(n_small)
    n_large_str = fmt_int(n_large)
    shift_small_str = fmt(shift_small, precision=1)
    shift_large_str = fmt(shift_large, precision=1)
    asym_large_str = fmt(asym_large, precision=1)
    gap_rate_str = fmt_percent(gap_rate, precision=1, style="prose")
    gap_present_str = fmt_percent(gap_present, precision=1, style="prose")
```

The regressional effect can be written out directly. Suppose a learned scorer reports an estimated utility $\EstimatedCandidateUtility_i = \CandidateUtility_i + \CandidateScoringError_i$ for candidate $\CandidateIndex$, where $\CandidateUtility_i$ is true task utility and $\CandidateScoringError_i$ is an independent scoring error with mean zero and standard deviation $\ScoringErrorStandardDeviation$ (scoring noise, distinct from the per-turn error rate in horizon compounding). Picking $\arg\max_i \EstimatedCandidateUtility_i$ maximizes the sum of utility and noise, so the winning candidate is disproportionately one that drew a large positive error. For independent Gaussian errors, the expected maximum error across $\CandidatePoolSize$ candidates scales for large $\CandidatePoolSize$ as

$$
\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\max_{i \le \CandidatePoolSize} \CandidateScoringError_i\Bigr] \approx \ScoringErrorStandardDeviation\sqrt{2\ln \CandidatePoolSize}
$$ {#eq-vol3-argmax-noise}

.[^fn-gumbel-tail-growth] In units of $\ScoringErrorStandardDeviation$, the exact expectation is `{python} ArgmaxSelection.shift_small_str` at `{python} ArgmaxSelection.n_small_str` candidates and `{python} ArgmaxSelection.shift_large_str` at `{python} ArgmaxSelection.n_large_str` candidates, where the asymptotic formula gives `{python} ArgmaxSelection.asym_large_str`. That expected maximum is an upper bound on the winner's expected scoring error, reached when all candidates have the same true utility. When true utilities vary, selection responds to both utility and noise (Exercise 8 derives the winner's error for a Gaussian utility model). An acceptance threshold calibrated on single, unselected completions therefore cannot be reused unmodified on argmax-selected winners.

[^fn-gumbel-tail-growth]: **Extreme-Value Asymptotics**: The form $\ScoringErrorStandardDeviation\sqrt{2\ln \CandidatePoolSize}$ is only the leading term of the Gaussian maximum, and convergence is slow, which is why the chapter computes the exact expectation beside it. The Gaussian is also a favorable case. Scoring errors with heavier tails, such as a learned judge that occasionally misjudges badly, push the selected error up faster than $\sqrt{\ln \CandidatePoolSize}$, so the drift in a real pool can exceed this estimate. \index{Extreme value!argmax selection}

A rising scoring error on the winner does not by itself mean that true utility is falling. In Exercise 8(b), independent Gaussian utility and noise make both the winner's expected utility and its expected scoring error rise with pool size. Empirical studies of best-of-$\CandidatePoolSize$ sampling under learned reward models show a sharper divergence: the proxy score keeps climbing while a held-out reference score rises, flattens, and then drops [@gao2023scaling]. That downturn comes from tail miscalibration or exploitable gaps in the proxy, not from @eq-vol3-argmax-noise alone. @Fig-vol3-goodhart-divergence sketches the pattern, with the winner's proxy score rising (dashed blue curve) while the held-out reference score peaks and turns down (solid green curve).

::: {#fig-vol3-goodhart-divergence fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Proxy and Reference Scores under Selection**: A qualitative sketch of the measured best-of-$\CandidatePoolSize$ pattern. The proxy score of the selected candidate keeps rising as $\CandidatePoolSize$ grows, while a held-out reference score rises and then declines. The widening gap illustrates proxy optimism under selection; the declining reference score is an empirical pattern, not a necessary consequence of growing scoring error. The axes carry no values, and the point where the reference score turns down depends on the task." fig-alt="Line sketch with candidates selected from, N, on a log-scale horizontal axis and score of the selected candidate on the vertical axis, without tick values. A dashed blue curve labeled proxy score rises and flattens. A solid green curve labeled held-out reference follows it at first, peaks near the middle at a marked dot, and then declines. The region between the curves is shaded, a red double-headed arrow at the right labels the gap scoring error of the winner, and a dashed line below the green peak notes that where the decline begins depends on the task."}
![](images/svg/goodhart_divergence.svg)
:::

Checker blind spots compound across large pools by the same binomial arithmetic as pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$. If an unmodeled edge case or loophole appears in a fraction $\ExploitCandidateFraction$ of single draws, a pool of $\CandidatePoolSize$ candidates contains at least one loophole-exploiting candidate with probability $1-(1-\ExploitCandidateFraction)^\CandidatePoolSize$. A loophole that shows up in only `{python} ArgmaxSelection.gap_rate_str` of individual samples, rare enough to miss during single-call testing, appears in a batch of `{python} ArgmaxSelection.n_large_str` candidates with probability `{python} ArgmaxSelection.gap_present_str`. Once a broken candidate slips through that loophole and receives a passing mark, competitive selection promotes it. Checker accuracy measured on unselected outputs therefore overstates accuracy under search, and the gap widens as the pool grows.

In the connection-pool repair, a patch can pass the test suite either by fixing the missing wake-up notification or by deleting the unit-test assertion that checks for blocked worker threads. Both edits raise the test score, and only the first fixes the bug. The candidate under test must therefore be isolated from the verifier so that generated code cannot edit test files or forge pass signals.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Grader isolation enforces this separation down to the candidate's process and interpreter, as developed in @sec-vol3-evaluation-gyms-grader-isolation.
:::

Isolating the grader stops tampering, but it does not widen what the test suite covers: a sealed regression suite still misses untested thread schedules, and a learned judge can still prefer confident, broken code. Evaluation must therefore test the outputs that the complete search policy produces at its deployed budget, counting false acceptances and abstentions explicitly. Adding confidence requires an independent check that covers a different failure mode rather than a second correlated scorer.

Verification also produces concrete intermediate facts that later turns can reuse, including refuted diagnoses, verified invariants, and passing test subsets. When a check refutes one assumption inside a multi-part candidate plan, the runtime does not need to throw away components that never depended on that assumption, provided it records which parts of the plan rest on which premises.

## Revising Candidate Plans {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-planning-revision}

When a targeted test refutes the initial diagnosis inside a multi-part repair plan, throwing away the entire plan wastes valid work such as API compatibility checks, whereas keeping the plan unchanged leaves the patch and test selection resting on a disproven premise. Suppose the repair agent forms a diagnosis, drafts a patch, checks public API constraints, and picks a test plan for a connection-pool leak, and a targeted test then refutes the diagnosis. To avoid both waste and stale conclusions, the runtime needs to identify which parts of the candidate depend on the refuted premise before deciding what the next model call should regenerate.

A **revisable candidate plan**\index{Revisable candidate plan!definition} records those dependencies explicitly. Instead of logging past actions, it tracks unexecuted candidate artifacts together with the evidence or upstream artifacts each one relies on. When new evidence refutes a premise, the runtime invalidates and regenerates only the affected subgraph while keeping supported artifacts intact, and the replacement artifacts then go through their own checks. This design comes directly from truth maintenance systems, which record explicit justifications for each conclusion so that retracting a premise automatically invalidates every step built on it [@doyle1979truth].

### Tracking dependencies inside a candidate {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-plan-graph}

Suppose the first repair candidate blames the connection-pool failure on an overly short client timeout. To know which parts of that candidate survive when a test refutes the timeout hypothesis, the runtime represents the candidate as a directed acyclic graph with a directed edge from each prerequisite to the artifact that depends on it (@tbl-vol3-candidate-plan-dependencies). Here the source excerpt, initial failure log, API declaration, and test inventory are supplied inputs, whereas the diagnosis, patch candidate, check selection, and API compatibility notes are generated artifacts. The graph records which components depend on which, whether or not the model generated them in that order.

| Artifact                | Direct prerequisites                        | What the artifact contributes                                     |
|:------------------------|:--------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Source excerpt          | Repository revision and file identity       | The implementation being considered                               |
| Diagnosis               | Source excerpt and failure observation      | A proposed explanation of the failure                             |
| Patch candidate         | Source excerpt and diagnosis                | A proposed change to that implementation                          |
| Test inventory          | Repository revision (a supplied input)      | The tests available for selection                                 |
| Check selection         | Patch candidate and test inventory          | Checks intended to distinguish this repair from an inadequate one |
| API compatibility notes | Task constraints and public API declaration | Restrictions that every acceptable repair must preserve           |
: **Dependencies within a repair candidate**: Each row names the inputs needed to interpret its artifact. A separate compatibility branch can be retained only while its own inputs remain applicable. {#tbl-vol3-candidate-plan-dependencies}

Now suppose the waiter-and-return test shows that an idle connection entered the pool while a waiting worker stayed blocked past the notification point. That observation refutes the timeout diagnosis and points to a missed wake-up notification instead. Because both the timeout patch and its check selection depend on the refuted diagnosis, the runtime marks them invalid and schedules them for replacement. The source excerpt stays valid because the repository file has not changed, and the API compatibility notes stay valid because the public interface constraints have not changed. The runtime builds the next prompt from the still-valid inputs plus the new test observation, asks for a new diagnosis, patch, and check selection, and runs checks on the new artifacts.

That selective reuse is only as sound as the recorded edges. A graph with a missing edge keeps stale conclusions just as an unmanaged prompt buffer does: if the compatibility notes silently depended on helper signatures that the new patch changes, leaving out that edge keeps broken compatibility claims in place. Dependency tracking pays off when maintaining the graph and walking its edges costs less in time and tokens than regenerating the unaffected branches from scratch.

### Invalidating stale and refuted evidence {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-precondition-invalidation}

Walking the dependency graph requires distinguishing an actively refuted claim from an observation whose preconditions no longer match the current candidate. A failing test directly refutes the claim that a patch fixes the bug, whereas a passing test from an earlier candidate remains a true record of what that earlier patch did while saying nothing about the edited patch now on the table. Reusing the earlier pass after the code changes would let an unverified edit slip through on stale evidence, whereas treating an expired observation as a direct contradiction would falsely rule out a working hypothesis.

To keep reuse sound, every recorded observation must carry its full provenance: the exact source revision or patch digest, test suite version, compiler flags, and runtime environment. Likewise, an observation from reading a file must bind to the cryptographic hash of the file contents when read, not to a file path whose contents a later step might overwrite.

When an input changes or a premise fails, the runtime marks that node unsupported and walks the directed edges to find every downstream artifact that needs review. If node $\InvalidatedArtifactNode$ loses support, the invalidated set is its reachable descendants in the graph: $\text{Desc}(\InvalidatedArtifactNode) = \{\ReachableArtifactNode \mid \InvalidatedArtifactNode \rightsquigarrow \ReachableArtifactNode\}$, where $\InvalidatedArtifactNode \rightsquigarrow \ReachableArtifactNode$ means a directed path runs from $\InvalidatedArtifactNode$ to $\ReachableArtifactNode$. Breadth-first search finds $\text{Desc}(\InvalidatedArtifactNode)$ in time linear in the vertices and edges.[^fn-make-rebuild-dependencies] Every node outside $\text{Desc}(\InvalidatedArtifactNode)$ keeps its support, including separate subgraphs such as the API compatibility notes. Walking a candidate graph of dozens or hundreds of nodes, like the one in @tbl-vol3-candidate-plan-dependencies, takes a negligible fraction of the illustrative `{python} ProbeAllocation.token_time_str` needed to decode a single token. The real engineering work is therefore recording the dependency edges accurately rather than traversing them. In the connection-pool repair, the waiter-and-return test contradicts the timeout diagnosis, and graph traversal marks its descendants (the patch and check selection) for review. The next call regenerates only the diagnosis and that branch from the retained inputs (@fig-vol3-plan-revision).

[^fn-make-rebuild-dependencies]: **Dependency-Driven Rebuilding**: Build tools solved the same problem for files. Make rebuilds a target only when one of its declared prerequisites is newer than the target [@feldman1979make], and its characteristic failure is the one described here, in which an undeclared dependency leaves a stale target that looks up to date. The saving is only as sound as the recorded edges. \index{Make!dependency tracking}

::: {#fig-vol3-plan-revision fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Invalidation and Scoped Regeneration**: In (A), the waiter-and-return test contradicts the timeout diagnosis. Following the recorded dependency edges marks the patch and check selection for review, while the recorded inputs and the separately derived API notes keep their support. In (B), a new request supplies that supported frontier and regenerates only the diagnosis, patch, and check selection. The graph records candidate artifacts, not executed operations, and each replacement must still pass its own checks. The test inventory that also feeds check selection is omitted." fig-alt="Two stacked panels with the same dependency graph. Inputs on the left are source excerpt, failure observation, waiter-return test, and API declaration. In panel A, source excerpt and failure observation feed a red diagnosis marked timeout too short, which feeds a patch candidate and then a check selection; source excerpt also feeds the patch candidate. The patch candidate and check selection are drawn with dashed red borders, labeled needs review, inside a dashed region labeled Desc of diagnosis. The waiter-return test points to the diagnosis with a dashed red arrow labeled contradicts. The API declaration feeds API notes labeled support kept. In panel B, a dashed blue region labeled regenerated contains diagnosis prime labeled missed notification, patch candidate prime labeled notify on return, and check selection prime labeled ordering test; the same inputs, now including the waiter-return test, feed diagnosis prime, and API notes are labeled retained."}
![](images/svg/fig-vol3-plan-revision.svg)
:::

Content hashes and environment digests make invalidation deterministic only when the recorded boundary captures every input that matters. An integration test that calls a live network service can change its outcome even when local files stay bit-identical, whereas editing an unrelated README file should not invalidate unit-test results whose code and inputs did not change. Sound reuse therefore depends on checking the full execution context (sandbox isolation, mocks, and declared inputs) rather than file timestamps or paths alone.

Candidate plans must also be kept separate from live environment state. The dependency graph tracks uncommitted candidate artifacts and their justifications; reading files, writing to disk, or running binaries in a sandbox changes real system state. Dropping an invalidated node from the plan graph does not roll back a modified file or free a running container, so the runtime must handle rollback and cleanup through separate recovery routines.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Compensation and cleanup of external effects that outlive an abandoned candidate branch are developed in @sec-vol3-failure-recovery-branch-compensation.
:::

### Choosing how much of a plan to regenerate {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-revision-mechanics}

Once graph traversal marks the invalidated nodes, the runtime must decide whether to replace a single node, rebuild its entire downstream subgraph, or stop deliberating altogether. Replacing a single step in isolation fails when the new artifact changes an interface that downstream steps rely on, whereas regenerating the whole plan from scratch wastes tokens and risks breaking parts that already worked. To scope a revision cleanly, the runtime builds a prompt with the task constraints, the still-valid upstream frontier, the observation that refuted the old step, and the exact nodes marked for replacement. In the connection-pool repair, the prompt asks for a new diagnosis, patch, and check selection while keeping the unchanged source excerpt and API notes. When the model returns replacement artifacts, the runtime checks both that they fit the retained artifacts and that their own prerequisites are met, because a locally valid replacement can still clash with preserved downstream nodes.

Depending on how much support the new observation removes, the runtime chooses among three responses. @Fig-vol3-hierarchical-revision orders these three responses around two questions, whether the dependents of the affected artifact still have their needs met and whether the task's own premises still hold:

1. A **local repair**\index{Local repair!definition} replaces a single node while keeping its interface and contracts unchanged so that its dependents stay valid, such as fixing a malformed shell flag in a test command without changing what the test checks.
2. A **subgraph resynthesis**\index{Subgraph resynthesis!definition} replaces a node and all of its descendants, feeding the model the intact upstream frontier and asking it to rebuild the path to the goal. In the connection-pool repair, this replaces the diagnosis, patch, and test selection while keeping the source excerpt and API compatibility notes.
3. **Stopping deliberation**\index{Stopping deliberation!definition} applies when new evidence refutes a premise of the task itself, such as a missing host library or credentials without write access. No plan revision can fix a broken task premise, so the runtime stops deliberating and escalates or reports the task unresolved instead of spending more tokens.

::: {#fig-vol3-hierarchical-revision fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Choosing the Revision Scope**: Two questions about the new evidence select among three responses. If the artifact's dependents still have what they need, a local repair replaces it alone. If they do not but the task's premises hold, subgraph resynthesis replaces the artifact and its descendants. If a premise has failed, deliberation stops and the task is reported unresolved or escalated. The tiers classify responses by how much support the evidence removes rather than establishing an unconditional preference for minimal edits." fig-alt="Flowchart. An amber box reading new evidence removes support from an artifact leads to a diamond asking whether dependents' needs are still met. Yes leads down to a card labeled local repair. No leads right to a second diamond asking whether task premises still hold. Yes leads down to a card labeled subgraph resynthesis. No leads by a red arrow to a red card labeled stop deliberation. Each card draws the same small dependency graph, a premise square feeding a chain of three artifact nodes and one side node. In local repair only the first chain node is filled and outlined as replaced, with the caption replace one artifact. In subgraph resynthesis the whole chain is filled and outlined, with the caption replace artifact plus descendants. In stop deliberation the premise square is red and every node is dashed, with the caption report unresolved or escalate. An arrow along the bottom runs from less support removed to more support removed."}
![](images/svg/hierarchical_revision_mechanics.svg)
:::

Smallest is not always best. When new evidence overturns an early framing assumption or the dependency graph has grown tangled, regenerating the whole candidate from scratch often produces a cleaner, more consistent result than patching a large subgraph, at the cost of re-emitting settled material and risking regressions in parts that already worked. Choosing between scoped revision and full regeneration weighs the share of the graph that was invalidated against the tokens, time, and checks needed to rebuild and verify the candidate.

```{python}
#| label: lego-candidate-plan-revision
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CANDIDATE PLAN REVISION OUTPUT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-revision-mechanics,
# │          nbk-03-compute-and-token-savings-of.
# │ Goal: Compare output tokens for full and scoped candidate regeneration.
# │ Show: Generated token counts, retained output share, and avoided output.
# │ How: Hypothetical equal-sized nodes; only replaced nodes are generated.
# │ Note: Excludes input processing, checks, scheduling, and physical effects.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check
from mlsysim.core.units import dimensionless

class PlanRevision:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    total_nodes = 12  # hypothetical complete candidate size
    replacement_nodes = 3  # hypothetical affected subset
    tokens_per_node = 150 * count  # hypothetical generated tokens per node

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    full_output = total_nodes * tokens_per_node
    local_output = replacement_nodes * tokens_per_node
    output_share = (local_output / full_output).to(dimensionless).magnitude
    avoided_share = 1 - output_share

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0 < replacement_nodes <= total_nodes, "replacement nodes within total")
    check(local_output <= full_output, "local output <= full output")
    check(0 <= avoided_share < 1, "avoided share in [0, 1)")

    # ┌── 4. EXPORT (Narrative Values) ─────────────────────────────────────
    total_nodes_str = fmt_count(total_nodes)
    replacement_nodes_str = fmt_count(replacement_nodes)
    tokens_per_node_str = fmt_tokens(tokens_per_node)
    full_output_str = fmt_tokens(full_output)
    local_output_str = fmt_tokens(local_output)
    output_share_str = fmt_percent(output_share, style="prose")
    avoided_share_str = fmt_percent(avoided_share, style="prose")
```

::: {#nbk-03-compute-and-token-savings-of .callout-notebook title="Output cost of a local plan revision"}

**Problem**: Suppose a candidate contains `{python} PlanRevision.total_nodes_str` nodes, each requiring `{python} PlanRevision.tokens_per_node_str` generated tokens. New evidence leaves `{python} PlanRevision.replacement_nodes_str` nodes needing replacement. How much output does scoped regeneration avoid if either approach produces a candidate adequate for the same subsequent checks?

**Math**: Multiplying the complete node count by the output per node gives `{python} PlanRevision.full_output_str` tokens for full regeneration. Multiplying the replacement count by the same output allowance gives `{python} PlanRevision.local_output_str` tokens for scoped regeneration. The scoped request generates `{python} PlanRevision.output_share_str` of the full request's output, avoiding `{python} PlanRevision.avoided_share_str` of that output under the equal-node-size assumption.

**Systems insight**: Scoped regeneration saves the exact fraction of the plan that keeps its support. That saving shrinks linearly as the refuted premise reaches more descendants and disappears when every node depends on it, so once most of the plan rests on the rejected premise, full regeneration costs little more and is simpler to check. This count covers generated plan tokens only; both options still pay for prompt input, integration, and verification checks.

:::

These output savings have to be weighed against the work of maintaining dependencies, building scoped prompts, and checking hybrid plans. Once a candidate plan passes verification and crosses into execution, it stops being an uncommitted candidate graph and becomes live workflow state that the harness executes and durable execution checkpoints across machine failures.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Persisting committed plan state across worker and infrastructure faults is developed in @sec-vol3-durable-execution.
:::

### Preventing revision thrashing {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-replanning-thrashing}

Even when each scoped revision saves tokens compared with full regeneration, a revision loop without stopping rules can still oscillate between two diagnoses, produce cosmetically different patches with the same bug, or regenerate plans in response to harmless compiler warnings. The runtime therefore checks whether a proposed revision responds to new evidence that actually refutes a premise, rather than treating every warning or score fluctuation as a reason to replan.

To prevent thrashing, the runtime enforces hard ceilings on model calls, total tokens, check runs, and wall-clock time. Every revision attempt, including a failed local repair, draws from that allowance, and the same ceilings bound the search as a whole (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-early-exit). When the budget runs out, the loop stops and reports the task unresolved or escalates to a human operator without merging the unverified patch. Seeing the same or structurally equivalent candidate under unchanged observations also triggers an immediate stop; revisiting an earlier idea is justified only when a new test observation has changed the evidence.

Dependency graphs let the runtime revise a single candidate without throwing away its valid parts, but an agent often holds several partial candidates at once. Deciding which partial candidate to extend next, how to keep concurrent branches from corrupting one another's workspaces, and when to stop searching altogether turns revision into bounded search.

## Bounded Search {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-bounded-search}

The repair agent now holds several partial candidates at once, some freshly revised and some untouched. At each step it can sample a fresh patch from the root, extend an existing partial candidate by one segment, or run a diagnostic probe to separate competing explanations. Every choice draws from the same task budget while creating different scheduling dependencies. A probe that gates the next code extension sits on the critical path. Independent candidate extensions can run in parallel across worker slots. Dropping a dead-end branch still forfeits the tokens and sandbox time already spent on it. A search policy therefore needs a pruning structure, workspace isolation between branches, separate accounts for tokens, time, and memory, reservations for in-flight work, and an ordered stopping rule.

### Where each search structure prunes {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-search-structures}

Search algorithms differ first in when they check and discard partial candidates. Flat sampling waits until the end: in best-of-$\CandidatePoolSize$, the runtime dispatches up to $\CandidatePoolSize$ independent generation calls and runs its selector only after all of them finish. Because the calls do not depend on one another, free serving capacity turns directly into lower latency through batching, provided the cluster can run all $\CandidatePoolSize$ streams without slowing per-token decoding. The price is that flat sampling defers all checking to the end, so a candidate with a broken premise in its first line still decodes to full length.

**Beam search**\index{Beam search!definition}[^fn-beam-search-harpy] moves that check inside the generation loop. The runtime keeps a frontier of at most $\BeamWidth$ partial candidates (the beam width). At each step it generates a fixed number of extensions per retained candidate, scores the extended prefixes, and keeps only the top $\BeamWidth$ survivors for the next step. If fewer than $\BeamWidth$ survive a check, only those survivors advance, and the root starts as a single prompt. Step scores can combine model log-probabilities, a learned process scorer, or a deterministic check. While $\BeamWidth$ caps the survivors carried between stages, peak memory during expansion must hold $\BeamWidth$ times the branching factor in active extensions along with their KV caches, scores, and parent pointers.

Pruning at each step trades generation tokens for scoring work and bets on the accuracy of the step scorer. If a noisy step score drops a prefix that would have led to a working patch, a fixed-width beam search never visits that branch again unless backtracking is added. Conversely, killing a broken prefix early saves all the tokens and final test runs its completion would have cost. Step pruning pays off when scoring costs less than the avoided downstream generation and the step check rarely rejects valid prefixes.

[^fn-beam-search-harpy]: **Beam Search**: The method first appeared in the HARPY speech recognition system, which advanced only a small set of the best-scoring partial paths at each step instead of the full search space [@lowerre1976]. It accepted a bounded risk of pruning the eventual best path in exchange for bounded time and memory, the same trade a runtime makes when it retains a fixed number of partial candidates. \index{Beam search!origin}

Rather than expanding every surviving candidate equally at every depth, tree search over intermediate reasoning steps [@yao2023tree] directs the next extension to whichever partial candidate looks most promising or most uncertain. **Monte Carlo tree search**\index{Monte Carlo tree search!definition} [@coulom2006efficient; @kocsis2006bandit] tracks visit counts and average leaf scores along the edges of the search tree. Its PUCT selection rule[^fn-puct-prior-bonus] from AlphaGo [@silver2016mastering] walks down from the root by picking at each partial state $\PolicyObservedState$ the extension $\PolicyAction$ that maximizes

$$
\TreeSearchMeanReturn(\PolicyObservedState,\PolicyAction) + \TreeSearchExplorationWeight\,\TreeSearchPriorDistribution(\PolicyAction \mid \PolicyObservedState)\,\frac{\sqrt{\sum_{\SiblingPolicyAction} \TreeSearchVisitCount(\PolicyObservedState,\SiblingPolicyAction)}}{1 + \TreeSearchVisitCount(\PolicyObservedState,\PolicyAction)},
$$ {#eq-vol3-puct}

where $\TreeSearchMeanReturn(\PolicyObservedState,\PolicyAction)$ is the mean leaf score seen on visits through extension $\PolicyAction$, $\TreeSearchVisitCount(\PolicyObservedState,\PolicyAction)$ is its visit count. The term $\TreeSearchPriorDistribution(\PolicyAction \mid \PolicyObservedState)$ is a prior distribution over extensions (such as the generator's probability for that step), and $\TreeSearchExplorationWeight$ is a positive weight that balances high-scoring branches against plausible, less-visited ones. The **leaf value** $\TreeSearchLeafScore$\index{Leaf value!definition} is the score assigned to a newly expanded partial candidate by a process scorer or step check, and $\TreeSearchMeanReturn$ averages those leaf values across visits. When a new leaf returns value $\TreeSearchLeafScore$, every edge along the path back to the root increments its visit count ($\TreeSearchVisitCount \leftarrow \TreeSearchVisitCount + 1$) and updates its running mean ($\TreeSearchMeanReturn \leftarrow \TreeSearchMeanReturn + (\TreeSearchLeafScore - \TreeSearchMeanReturn)/\TreeSearchVisitCount$). If $\TreeSearchLeafScore$ comes from a noisy learned scorer, $\TreeSearchMeanReturn$ inherits the selection optimism of @eq-vol3-argmax-noise and pulls future visits toward branches whose early scores were inflated by noise. Tree search therefore helps only when its smarter allocation saves more work than leaf scoring and tree bookkeeping add.

[^fn-puct-prior-bonus]: **From UCT to PUCT**: The UCT rule treated each node's choice of extension as a multi-armed bandit, adding an exploration bonus that shrinks as an extension accumulates visits [@kocsis2006bandit]. PUCT weights that bonus by a predictor's prior over the arms [@rosin2011multi], which is what lets a language model's own step probabilities concentrate a small budget on plausible extensions. A miscalibrated prior steers visits away from correct but unlikely steps just as effectively. \index{Monte Carlo tree search!PUCT}

The three structures differ in where they prune (@fig-vol3-search-topologies). Best-of-$\CandidatePoolSize$ waits until all candidates finish, beam search prunes at every step boundary, and tree search expands one favored leaf at a time while updating visit counts and mean values along its path. Those pruning points set each structure's concurrency, live state, and prefix sharing (@tbl-vol3-search-topologies).

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Radix prefix caching, which lets later requests for a branch reuse the KV state of its shared ancestors, is developed in @sec-vol3-kv-cache-radix-lookup.
:::

::: {#fig-vol3-search-topologies data-explore="mechanism-scene" data-explore-key="vol3:fig-vol3-search-topologies" fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Where Each Search Structure Prunes**: Best-of-$\CandidatePoolSize$ generates complete candidates independently and discards all but the selected one only at the end. Beam search generates the beam width times the extensions per candidate at each step, scores them, and keeps the beam width. Tree search expands the leaf its selection rule favors, evaluates it, and updates visit counts and value estimates along the path to the root. The drawings show structure only; the pool size, beam width, and depth are illustrative." fig-alt="Three panels of node diagrams. Best-of-N: a prompt node branches into four chains of three generated nodes each; past a dashed line labeled select, one final node is marked selected and three are marked pruned. Beam: a prompt node branches into two nodes, each of which generates two children; a dashed line labeled score, keep 2 marks two children pruned, the two survivors each generate two more, and a second dashed line labeled keep 2 marks two retained and two pruned. Tree search: an uneven tree in which one path from the prompt is drawn bold and ends at a new leaf labeled evaluated V, with a note that the bold path updates N sub visit, the visit count, and Q; other nodes are drawn dashed as not yet expanded. A legend identifies prompt, generated, retained or selected, generated then pruned, and not yet expanded nodes."}
![](images/svg/search_topologies_comparison.svg)
:::

| **Structure**                | **Where pruning happens**                | **Concurrency**                               | **Search state**                                         | **Prefix sharing**                       |
|:-----------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------|
| Best-of-$\CandidatePoolSize$ | After complete candidates, at selection  | All $\CandidatePoolSize$ requests independent | $\CandidatePoolSize$ candidates and their check results  | The common prompt only                   |
| Beam                         | At each step boundary, by step score     | Within a step; stages wait for scoring        | Up to width times extensions before pruning, plus scores | Each retained prefix with its extensions |
| Tree search                  | Adaptively, by value estimate and visits | Irregular; depends on which leaves are chosen | Tree nodes with visit counts and value estimates         | Every node's ancestors along its path    |

: **Search structures compared**: Each structure moves the pruning decision to a different point and holds different state. Concurrency describes the dependency graph; actual overlap depends on service capacity. {#tbl-vol3-search-topologies tbl-colwidths="[13,22,21,23,21]"}

### How step pruning bounds tree growth {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-tree-growth}

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-pruned-tree
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PRUNED TREE GROWTH (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-tree-growth.
# │ Goal: Show how a step check's rejection rate bounds expected tree size.
# │ Show: Unpruned leaf explosion; effective branching factor; generated nodes.
# │ How: Independent rejection of each child; generated nodes are b times the
# │      surviving parents at each depth; equal-sized steps.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

class PrunedTree:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    wide_b = 4  # hypothetical alternatives per step, unpruned illustration
    wide_depth = 10  # hypothetical steps, unpruned illustration
    b = 5  # hypothetical children proposed per retained node
    p_prune = 0.68  # hypothetical probability a step check rejects a child
    depth = 3  # hypothetical steps in the worked example

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    wide_leaves = wide_b**wide_depth
    b_eff = b * (1 - p_prune)
    critical_prune = 1 - 1 / b
    unpruned_generated = 0
    pruned_generated = 0.0
    for d in range(1, depth + 1):
        unpruned_generated += b**d
        pruned_generated += b * b_eff ** (d - 1)
    unpruned_leaves = b**depth
    pruned_leaves = b_eff**depth
    generated_saving = 1 - pruned_generated / unpruned_generated

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(wide_leaves > 1_000_000, "Unpruned illustration exceeds a million leaves")
    check(b_eff > 1, "Worked example remains supercritical")
    check(p_prune < critical_prune, "Rejection rate is below the subcritical threshold")
    check(pruned_generated < unpruned_generated, "Pruning reduces generated nodes")
    check(generated_saving > p_prune, "Node saving exceeds the per-child rejection rate")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    wide_b_str = fmt_int(wide_b)
    wide_depth_str = fmt_int(wide_depth)
    wide_leaves_str = fmt_int(wide_leaves)
    b_str = fmt_int(b)
    p_prune_str = fmt_percent(p_prune, precision=0, style="prose")
    depth_str = fmt_int(depth)
    b_eff_str = fmt(b_eff, precision=1)
    critical_prune_str = fmt_percent(critical_prune, precision=0, style="prose")
    unpruned_generated_str = fmt_int(unpruned_generated)
    pruned_generated_str = fmt(pruned_generated, precision=1)
    unpruned_leaves_str = fmt_int(unpruned_leaves)
    pruned_leaves_str = fmt(pruned_leaves, precision=1)
    generated_saving_str = fmt_percent(generated_saving, precision=1, style="prose")
```

A search tree that expands every node into `{python} PrunedTree.wide_b_str` branches across `{python} PrunedTree.wide_depth_str` steps without pruning produces `{python} PrunedTree.wide_leaves_str` leaves and quickly exhausts memory and token budgets. Step pruning bounds that growth. Suppose each retained node proposes $\SearchBranchingFactor$ child extensions and a step check independently rejects each child with probability $\ChildPruningProbability$. The expected number of surviving children per expanded node, the **effective branching factor**\index{Effective branching factor!definition}, is

$$
\EffectiveBranchingFactor = \SearchBranchingFactor\,(1 - \ChildPruningProbability).
$$ {#eq-vol3-effective-branching}

Under @eq-vol3-effective-branching, the expected frontier width at depth $\SearchDepthIndex$ is $\EffectiveBranchingFactor^{\,\SearchDepthIndex}$. Because each surviving node at depth $\SearchDepthIndex-1$ generates and checks $\SearchBranchingFactor$ children, the expected total number of generated nodes through depth $\SearchDepth$ is $\sum_{\SearchDepthIndex=1}^{\SearchDepth} \SearchBranchingFactor\,\EffectiveBranchingFactor^{\,\SearchDepthIndex-1}$. This is a Galton–Watson branching process.[^fn-galton-watson-extinction] When $\EffectiveBranchingFactor < 1$, which requires a rejection rate above $1 - 1/\SearchBranchingFactor$, the frontier shrinks geometrically with depth and dies out on its own. When $\EffectiveBranchingFactor > 1$, the expected frontier still grows exponentially, so hard ceilings on depth, tokens, or time must stop the search.

[^fn-galton-watson-extinction]: **Galton–Watson Process**: The model comes from a Victorian question about the extinction of family surnames, analyzed in 1875 [@watson1875probability]. That analysis wrongly concluded that every line dies out; the correct result is the threshold used here, under which extinction is certain when the mean number of surviving offspring is at most one (excluding the degenerate case of exactly one child every time) and avoidable when it exceeds one. For a search tree the surviving offspring are the children that pass the step check, so the rejection rate decides which side of the threshold the search lands on. \index{Galton–Watson process!search trees}

Suppose each node proposes `{python} PrunedTree.b_str` extensions, the step check rejects `{python} PrunedTree.p_prune_str` of them, and the search runs to depth `{python} PrunedTree.depth_str`. The effective branching factor is `{python} PrunedTree.b_eff_str`. Because the `{python} PrunedTree.p_prune_str` rejection rate sits below the critical rate of `{python} PrunedTree.critical_prune_str` for $\SearchBranchingFactor =$ `{python} PrunedTree.b_str`, the tree remains supercritical ($\EffectiveBranchingFactor > 1$). Even so, an unpruned tree across three steps generates `{python} PrunedTree.unpruned_generated_str` nodes and ends with `{python} PrunedTree.unpruned_leaves_str` leaves. The pruned tree generates an expected `{python} PrunedTree.pruned_generated_str` nodes and ends with `{python} PrunedTree.pruned_leaves_str` leaves, cutting node generations by `{python} PrunedTree.generated_saving_str`. The total saving beats the `{python} PrunedTree.p_prune_str` single-step rejection rate because rejecting a parent also removes the entire subtree beneath it. With equal-sized steps, generated tokens drop by the same fraction, though each rejected node still pays for its own generation and step check.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_ttc_margin_pruned_nodes.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Three horizontal orange bars of nodes generated. Unpruned: 155. A dashed, lightly filled reference bar for a flat 68 percent cut is about one third as long. Pruned: 25.8, about half the length of the reference bar."}

*Each rejected child also removes the subtree it would have grown.*
:::

Two practical limits qualify this calculation. First, a step check that falsely rejects valid steps kills good branches permanently, so aggressive pruning helps only when false rejections are rare. Second, when a step needs just one surviving child to move forward, proposing children one at a time takes $1/(1 - \ChildPruningProbability)$ tries in expectation, whereas proposing a batch of $\ChildBatchSize$ children in parallel takes $1/(1 - \ChildPruningProbability^{\,\ChildBatchSize})$ rounds of $\ChildBatchSize$ children each. Batching cuts wall-clock rounds at the price of generating more total children, the same latency-versus-work trade that notebook \ref{nbk-03-best-of-n-pool-price} priced for best-of-$\CandidatePoolSize$ sampling.

### Isolating workspaces across search branches {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-mutable-sandbox-search}

If one search branch edits files in a shared workspace and a sibling branch then runs its tests against that modified working tree, the sibling's test results no longer reflect its own proposed patch. Although a partial candidate is just data in memory while being decoded, testing it requires running code against a real filesystem and process state. Every branch that writes files or mutates state therefore needs its own isolated container, copy-on-write filesystem snapshot, or deterministic rollback before another branch runs, so that each observation belongs strictly to the candidate and workspace snapshot that produced it.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Copy-on-write task workspaces that keep each run's file modifications private are developed in @sec-vol3-sandboxes-cow-provisioning.
:::

Isolating branches costs real system resources even when most branches are later pruned. Concurrent sandboxes consume host RAM, disk volumes, process slots, and network bandwidth, while their test logs accumulate in the runtime's state. Even read-only diagnostic commands need sandboxed permissions so they cannot leak host credentials or environment variables into the search trace. Pruning a branch drops it from the search frontier, but backtracking in the search tree cannot unsent an outbound network call or undo a write to an external database. Sandbox boundaries block those external writes during search, and any external action the runtime does permit has to be budgeted as irreversible.

### Accounting for the whole search {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-search-accounting}

Collapsing tokens, test runtimes, and memory into a single composite "search cost" hides whichever physical limit the search will hit first, because a beam search that cuts generated output tokens nearly in half can still cost more in dollars once repeated prompt reads are counted. A search runtime therefore keeps four separate accounts: money spent, physical work by unit, elapsed wall-clock time, and peak live state. Money is the one common unit that adds up across generator tokens, scorer calls, and tool runs. Physical work, by contrast, comes in non-interchangeable kinds: prompt tokens, output tokens, scorer tokens, test executions, and sandbox startups each load different hardware resources, and adding model FLOPs to test seconds produces a meaningless number.

Wall-clock time depends on how the scheduler maps those operations onto hardware: sequential stages add along the critical path, concurrent branches overlap up to the available worker slots, and requests beyond those slots wait in waves. Peak live state is a fourth, separate limit, set by what must sit in memory and storage at the same instant (active KV caches, candidate trees, test logs, and live sandboxes) rather than the cumulative work over the whole run. Saving output tokens by pruning early often adds prompt re-reads, scoring barriers, or concurrent state, so keeping the four accounts separate shows which resource actually constrains the policy.

```{python}
#| label: lego-bounded-search-accounts
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ BOUNDED SEARCH RESOURCE ACCOUNTS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-bounded-search,
# │          nbk-03-compute-allocation-and-latency-trade-offs.
# │ Goal: Compare counted work, token charges, and scheduled time for two
# │       hypothetical policies without assigning either a quality advantage.
# │ Show: Expansion counts, input/output/scorer tokens, prices, and time.
# │ How: Registry-derived output allowance; explicit local workload, prices,
# │      concurrency, and nonoverlapping generation/scoring/test stages.
# │ Note: No prefix-reuse discount. Prefill and service overheads are omitted
# │       from the timing subtotal, not from generator input-token charges.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import BYTES_INT8, dimensionless, param
from math import ceil

class SearchBudget:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    accel = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    weight_bytes = BYTES_INT8
    steps = 4  # hypothetical candidate length in equal-sized segments
    step_tokens = 128  # hypothetical newly generated tokens per extension
    prompt_tokens = 4096  # hypothetical common task prompt per request
    flat_candidates = 16  # hypothetical complete-candidate budget
    beam_width = 4  # hypothetical retained-prefix limit
    extensions = 3  # hypothetical extensions per retained prefix
    generation_slots = 8  # hypothetical concurrent streams, unchanged rate
    test_slots = 8  # hypothetical concurrent isolated test runs
    score_time = 15 * ms  # fixed scenario allowance per FULL-prefix score
    test_time = 0.5 * second  # fixed scenario allowance per final test
    price_in = 3 * USD / (MILLION * count)  # hypothetical generator input rate
    price_out = 15 * USD / (MILLION * count)  # hypothetical output rate
    price_score = 0.50 * USD / (MILLION * count)  # hypothetical scorer input rate

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    weights = model.parameters / param * weight_bytes
    token_time = (weights / accel.memory.bandwidth).to(second)
    retained = 1
    frontier_counts = []
    beam_prompt_tokens = 0
    scorer_tokens = 0
    beam_waves = 0
    for depth in range(1, steps + 1):
        expanded = retained * extensions
        frontier_counts.append(expanded)
        beam_prompt_tokens += expanded * (prompt_tokens + (depth - 1) * step_tokens)
        # The scorer reads each complete generated prefix, not only its suffix.
        scorer_tokens += expanded * depth * step_tokens
        beam_waves += ceil(expanded / generation_slots)
        retained = min(beam_width, expanded)
    beam_segments = sum(frontier_counts)
    beam_output_tokens = beam_segments * step_tokens
    flat_length = steps * step_tokens
    flat_output_tokens = flat_candidates * flat_length
    flat_prompt_tokens = flat_candidates * prompt_tokens
    flat_waves = ceil(flat_candidates / generation_slots)
    flat_test_waves = ceil(flat_candidates / test_slots)
    beam_test_waves = ceil(retained / test_slots)
    flat_generation_time = flat_waves * flat_length * token_time
    beam_generation_time = beam_waves * step_tokens * token_time
    beam_scoring_time = beam_segments * score_time
    flat_elapsed = flat_generation_time + flat_test_waves * test_time
    beam_elapsed = beam_generation_time + beam_scoring_time + beam_test_waves * test_time
    flat_token_cost = flat_prompt_tokens * count * price_in + flat_output_tokens * count * price_out
    beam_token_cost = beam_prompt_tokens * count * price_in + beam_output_tokens * count * price_out + scorer_tokens * count * price_score
    output_saving = 1 - beam_output_tokens / flat_output_tokens
    # Break-even: the input-price fraction (e.g. under prefix caching) at which
    # the beam's output saving net of scoring pays for its repeated input.
    out_saving_usd = ((flat_output_tokens - beam_output_tokens) * count * price_out).to(USD)
    scorer_usd = (scorer_tokens * count * price_score).to(USD)
    input_premium_usd = ((beam_prompt_tokens - flat_prompt_tokens) * count * price_in).to(USD)
    breakeven_input_share = ((out_saving_usd - scorer_usd) / input_premium_usd).to(dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(frontier_counts == [3, 9, 12, 12], "Root expansion precedes a full beam")
    check(beam_segments == 36 and retained == 4, "Count extensions before pruning")
    check(flat_output_tokens == 8192 and beam_output_tokens == 4608, "Count generated suffixes once")
    check(scorer_tokens == 13440, "Full-prefix scoring rereads ancestor tokens")
    check(beam_prompt_tokens == 156288 and flat_prompt_tokens == 65536, "Bill every supplied prompt without reuse discount")
    check(beam_waves == 7 and flat_waves == 2, "Apply generation concurrency to each stage")
    check(abs(output_saving - 0.4375) < 1e-12, "Beam generates fewer output tokens in this scenario")
    check(beam_token_cost > flat_token_cost, "Repeated inputs reverse the token-charge ranking")
    check(0 < breakeven_input_share < 1, "Beam breaks even only at a discounted input price")
    check(22 * second < flat_elapsed < 23 * second, "Flat timing subtotal remains in its stated range")
    check(19 * second < beam_elapsed < 21 * second, "Beam timing subtotal remains in its stated range")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    steps_str = fmt_count(steps)
    step_tokens_str = fmt_count(step_tokens)
    prompt_tokens_str = fmt_count(prompt_tokens)
    flat_candidates_str = fmt_count(flat_candidates)
    beam_width_str = fmt_count(beam_width)
    extensions_str = fmt_count(extensions)
    generation_slots_str = fmt_count(generation_slots)
    test_slots_str = fmt_count(test_slots)
    token_time_ms_str = fmt_time(token_time, unit=ms, precision=3)
    score_time_ms_str = fmt_time(score_time, unit=ms, precision=0)
    test_time_s_str = fmt_time(test_time, unit=second, precision=1)
    price_in_str = fmt_usd(price_in * MILLION * count, precision=0)
    price_out_str = fmt_usd(price_out * MILLION * count, precision=0)
    price_score_str = fmt_usd(price_score * MILLION * count, precision=2)
    frontier_counts_str = MarkdownStr(", ".join(str(n) for n in frontier_counts))
    beam_segments_str = fmt_count(beam_segments)
    flat_length_str = fmt_count(flat_length)
    flat_output_tokens_str = fmt_count(flat_output_tokens)
    beam_output_tokens_str = fmt_count(beam_output_tokens)
    flat_prompt_tokens_str = fmt_count(flat_prompt_tokens)
    beam_prompt_tokens_str = fmt_count(beam_prompt_tokens)
    scorer_tokens_str = fmt_count(scorer_tokens)
    flat_waves_str = fmt_count(flat_waves)
    beam_waves_str = fmt_count(beam_waves)
    flat_test_waves_str = fmt_count(flat_test_waves)
    beam_test_waves_str = fmt_count(beam_test_waves)
    beam_scoring_time_s_str = fmt_time(beam_scoring_time, unit=second, precision=2)
    flat_elapsed_s_str = fmt_time(flat_elapsed, unit=second, precision=2)
    beam_elapsed_s_str = fmt_time(beam_elapsed, unit=second, precision=2)
    flat_token_cost_str = fmt_usd(flat_token_cost, precision=4)
    beam_token_cost_str = fmt_usd(beam_token_cost, precision=4)
    output_saving_pct_str = fmt_percent(output_saving, precision=2, style="prose")
    input_premium_usd_str = fmt_usd(input_premium_usd, precision=3)
    out_saving_usd_str = fmt_usd(out_saving_usd, precision=3)
    breakeven_input_share_str = fmt_percent(breakeven_input_share, precision=1, style="prose")
```

::: {#nbk-03-compute-allocation-and-latency-trade-offs .callout-notebook title="Flat sampling vs. bounded beam expansion"}

**Problem**: A coding agent generates candidate patches in `{python} SearchBudget.steps_str` segments of `{python} SearchBudget.step_tokens_str` tokens.
