Compare `{python} SearchBudget.flat_candidates_str` complete candidates with beam width `{python} SearchBudget.beam_width_str` and `{python} SearchBudget.extensions_str` extensions per retained prefix. How do early pruning and repeated scoring change the resource totals?

**Setup**: Every generator request supplies the same `{python} SearchBudget.prompt_tokens_str`-token task prompt plus its retained generated prefix. The illustrative per-token generation time from @sec-vol3-foundation-model-per-call-work-estimate is `{python} SearchBudget.token_time_ms_str`. Assume `{python} SearchBudget.generation_slots_str` generation streams can maintain that rate concurrently. The scorer reads the entire generated prefix, excluding the common task prompt, and processes requests serially at a fixed `{python} SearchBudget.score_time_ms_str` per request regardless of prefix length. The growth with prefix length that @eq-vol3-prm-rescoring describes therefore appears in the scorer's token bill rather than in this stipulated time. Each final test takes `{python} SearchBudget.test_time_s_str`, with `{python} SearchBudget.test_slots_str` isolated runs available concurrently. Generation, scoring, and final testing do not overlap in this schedule.

Hypothetical prices per million tokens are `{python} SearchBudget.price_in_str` for generator input, `{python} SearchBudget.price_out_str` for output, and `{python} SearchBudget.price_score_str` for scorer input. Input charges include every supplied token, without a prefix-reuse discount. The timing subtotal omits prefill, queueing, request transfer, workspace preparation, and cleanup. It is not a prediction of complete service latency, and the token-charge subtotal excludes execution and infrastructure charges.

**Math**: Multiplying `{python} SearchBudget.flat_candidates_str` candidates by `{python} SearchBudget.flat_length_str` output tokens per candidate gives `{python} SearchBudget.flat_output_tokens_str` output tokens. Multiplying the same candidate count by the common prompt length gives `{python} SearchBudget.flat_prompt_tokens_str` input tokens. Generation occupies `{python} SearchBudget.flat_waves_str` waves of complete candidates, followed by `{python} SearchBudget.flat_test_waves_str` test waves. Multiplying the generation waves by candidate length and the per-token allowance, then adding the test waves times test duration, gives `{python} SearchBudget.flat_elapsed_s_str`. Multiplying each token count by its corresponding price gives a token-charge subtotal of `{python} SearchBudget.flat_token_cost_str`.

The beam expands frontiers of `{python} SearchBudget.frontier_counts_str` extensions in successive stages. Adding these counts gives `{python} SearchBudget.beam_segments_str` newly generated segments; multiplying by the segment length gives `{python} SearchBudget.beam_output_tokens_str` output tokens. After each stage it retains at most the beam width. For each request, generator input is the common prompt plus the preceding generated segments; summing across requests gives `{python} SearchBudget.beam_prompt_tokens_str` input tokens. The scorer instead reads each complete generated prefix, including its new segment. Summing each stage's extension count times its prefix length gives `{python} SearchBudget.scorer_tokens_str` scorer-input tokens. Generation requires `{python} SearchBudget.beam_waves_str` waves of one-segment requests; serial scoring adds `{python} SearchBudget.beam_scoring_time_s_str`; the final survivors fit in `{python} SearchBudget.beam_test_waves_str` test wave. Applying the same duration and price arithmetic gives `{python} SearchBudget.beam_elapsed_s_str` and `{python} SearchBudget.beam_token_cost_str`.

**Systems insight**: The beam generates `{python} SearchBudget.output_saving_pct_str` fewer output tokens, worth `{python} SearchBudget.out_saving_usd_str`, but resupplying the task prompt and retained prefixes to every extension costs `{python} SearchBudget.input_premium_usd_str` more in input, so its token bill is the higher one. The knob is the price of repeated input. The beam's bill falls below flat sampling's only when input tokens cost less than `{python} SearchBudget.breakeven_input_share_str` of list price, the regime a prefix cache creates. Its shorter generation waves already give it the lower timing subtotal under this schedule, before omitted prefill is added back. Quality does not appear in these totals; the choice between the two rests on the check results each produces.

:::

### Reserving budget before admitting work {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-admission-limits}

Checking how many tokens a search has spent only after concurrent model calls return is too late to prevent a budget overrun, because eight in-flight calls can all finish and bill their full output allowance before the budget account updates. Before dispatching any candidate extension, the runtime must reserve the call's maximum allowed output tokens along with its scorer and sandbox allowances, keep settled spend plus open reservations below the search ceilings, and release unused capacity only after the call settles. A post-call usage receipt tells the runtime what to settle, but only a pre-dispatch reservation can bound concurrent spend in advance.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Charging every pending operation its worst-case ceiling until settlement is the bounded-liability admission developed in @sec-vol3-agent-harness-reservation-settlement.
:::

Search depth and wall-clock time also need separate limits. A depth cap limits the chain of sequential extensions or tool turns, while a deadline caps user-perceived latency. When the deadline expires, the runtime stops admitting new work, drops late responses from the expired phase, and sends cancellation signals to in-flight calls. As @sec-vol3-foundation-model-streaming-cancellation showed, however, sending a cancel request does not guarantee that the remote server stops immediately; a server that ignores cancellation can keep decoding and billing up to the call's full output ceiling. Until the remote service settles the request, the runtime must keep the full reservation charged against the budget.

Running out of budget ends the search without lowering the acceptance bar. A finished candidate can still fail regression tests, and a high learned score cannot stand in for a required check pass. If no candidate meets the acceptance contract when a ceiling is reached, the runtime reports an incomplete result, abstains, or escalates to a human operator. That separation is invariant closure (principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}) applied to deliberation: mechanical limits sit below the model to stop spending, and acceptance evidence sits above the model to authorize returning an answer.

### When to stop searching early {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-early-exit}

Hard ceilings stop a search when its allowance runs out, whereas early-stopping rules end the search inside the ceilings as soon as a candidate passes or the next round is no longer worth its cost. Many repair workloads need only the first candidate that meets their acceptance criteria, a stopping rule known as **satisficing**\index{Satisficing!definition}.[^fn-satisficing-aspiration-level] Once a candidate passes the required checks and policy rules, the search stops and returns it. If the search stage checks only compilation, stopping at the first compiling patch hands testing and deployment authorization to the next stage of the pipeline.

[^fn-satisficing-aspiration-level]: **Satisficing**: Herbert Simon borrowed the word in 1956 to describe a chooser who stops at the first alternative meeting an aspiration level, because a decision maker with limited capacity cannot afford an exhaustive search for the best [@simon1956rational]. A runtime's acceptance criteria play the role of that aspiration level, which is why they must be fixed before search begins rather than lowered as the budget runs out. \index{Satisficing!origin}

An explicit secondary objective can justify searching further after finding an acceptable candidate, such as looking for a smaller diff or a faster query plan within the remaining budget. A rising learned score by itself does not justify continuing if held-out benchmarks show that higher scores past the pass threshold rarely improve real outcomes. Continuing therefore requires an explicit estimate of what the next unit of work is worth.

**Marginal stopping**\index{Marginal stopping!definition}[^fn-sprt-sequential-stopping] asks whether the expected acceptance gain from the next round is worth its added cost. During a live repair, the runtime does not know the exact probability that the next attempt will pass, so it estimates that gain from calibration curves measured on held-out tasks or from progress signals such as fewer failing tests. Because any single diagnostic is only a partial signal, those estimates hold only for workloads and test suites similar to the calibration set.

[^fn-sprt-sequential-stopping]: **Sequential Stopping**: Statistics made stopping part of an experiment's design with the sequential probability ratio test, which after each observation decides whether to accept, reject, or sample again [@wald1945sequential]. Such tests reach a verdict with fewer observations on average than a fixed-size test with the same error rates. The marginal rule borrows that structure, although its threshold is an economic choice rather than an error rate. \index{Sequential probability ratio test!stopping}

For a nested sequence of round limits under the same workload and acceptance criterion, let $\CalibratedAcceptanceEstimate_{\AdmittedWorkUnitCount}$ estimate the probability of finding an acceptable result by round $\AdmittedWorkUnitCount$. Let $\CumulativeWorkCost_{\AdmittedWorkUnitCount}$ denote the expected cumulative expenditure of the policy that stops at its first acceptable result and otherwise runs up to that round limit. Before admitting round $\AdmittedWorkUnitCount$, with no earlier acceptance, the marginal policy stops when

$$
\frac{\CalibratedAcceptanceEstimate_{\AdmittedWorkUnitCount} - \CalibratedAcceptanceEstimate_{\AdmittedWorkUnitCount-1}}{\CumulativeWorkCost_{\AdmittedWorkUnitCount} - \CumulativeWorkCost_{\AdmittedWorkUnitCount-1}} < \MarginalStoppingThreshold,
$$ {#eq-vol3-marginal-stopping}

where $\MarginalStoppingThreshold$ is the minimum required gain in acceptance probability per unit of spend. The denominator is the cost of admitting round $\AdmittedWorkUnitCount$ multiplied by the probability of reaching round $\AdmittedWorkUnitCount$ without an earlier pass. Dividing the numerator by that same reach probability gives the conditional chance of passing in round $\AdmittedWorkUnitCount$ given earlier failure. The ratio in @eq-vol3-marginal-stopping therefore equals the conditional next-round pass probability divided by the full cost of running that round. Dividing the unconditional probability gain by the full round cost would mix two different denominators. In an adaptive search, these conditional estimates should be updated from the current search state rather than read blindly from an unconditional table.

The numerator measures the gain in the estimated chance of a verified pass, not the number of new candidates or a rise in a heuristic score. The verification asymmetry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}) explains why, since generating more candidates and obtaining a verified solution are distinct events. A search whose calibrated chance of passing stays flat is burning budget without making progress, no matter how many tokens it emits. The threshold $\MarginalStoppingThreshold$ is an economic choice set by the value of an automated fix relative to human escalation, net of checker error and delay; high failure costs never justify searching longer against an untrustworthy check.

For satisficing workloads, the runtime applies these three stopping checks in a fixed order before admitting any new work (@fig-vol3-stopping-boundaries). First, hard ceilings on tokens, calls, depth, or wall-clock time stop new admissions unconditionally; if an acceptable candidate is already in hand it goes to the acceptance gate, and otherwise the runtime abstains or escalates. Second, within the ceilings, any candidate that meets the acceptance criteria stops the search and goes to the acceptance gate. Third, when the ceilings still have room and no candidate has passed yet, the marginal stopping rule (@eq-vol3-marginal-stopping) stops the search early if the next round's expected gain per dollar falls below $\MarginalStoppingThreshold$. Reversing this order would either let an optimistic gain estimate breach a hard ceiling or let a diminishing-returns check discard a candidate that already passed. Whichever condition ends the search, the runtime settles all open reservations and separates verified passes from unverified attempts.

::: {#fig-vol3-stopping-boundaries fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Stopping Precedence**: Before admitting more work, the runtime tests three conditions in a fixed order. A hard ceiling on tokens, calls, depth, or time stops new admissions, preserving any already acceptable candidate for the acceptance decision. Within the ceilings, a candidate that meets the acceptance criteria ends search and goes to the acceptance decision, which stopping does not itself make. Only then does the marginal rule compare the gain per unit cost with $\MarginalStoppingThreshold$. A stop without an acceptable candidate is reported as incomplete or escalated, never returned as accepted." fig-alt="Flowchart. A box reading before admitting more work leads to three diamonds in sequence: 1, hard ceiling reached; 2, acceptance criteria met; 3, gain per cost below epsilon stop. A no from the first two passes to the next diamond. A no from the third leads up to a box reading admit next work, which loops back to the start. Each yes leads down to an outcome card: stop new work, listing tokens, calls, depth, and time and reading keep acceptable candidate, else incomplete or escalate; stop search, reading return the candidate for the acceptance decision; and stop early, reading further work not worth its cost, report incomplete or escalate."}
![](images/svg/search_stopping_boundaries.svg)
:::

::: {#chk-03-search-topologies .callout-checkpoint title="Accounting for a bounded search"}

The resource accounts and the stopping policy must count work even when it produces no accepted result.

- [ ] **Input budget**: Using the notebook's prompt length and expansion counts, estimate the input tokens spent on common prompts alone and explain why they exceed flat sampling's input count.
- [ ] **Pending work**: Which requests must remain reserved when the runtime reaches its deadline but remote cancellation is unconfirmed?
- [ ] **Stopping precedence**: A search has nearly exhausted its token ceiling, holds a candidate that passes the sealed suite, and still estimates a marginal gain above $\MarginalStoppingThreshold$. Which rule decides, and what does the runtime do next?
- [ ] **Acceptance evidence**: What evidence would justify stopping with an accepted repair, and what should the runtime return if only the highest learned score is available?

:::

Search structures, resource accounts, and stopping rules define how a single deliberation policy runs inside its bounds. Choosing among competing policies requires comparing their end-to-end pass rates, actual spend, and deadline completions on the same workload, charging every failed and timed-out attempt to the accepted results.

## Evaluating Deliberation Policies {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-strategy-design}

Suppose an iterative search policy resolves more connection-pool failures than a single-call baseline. That gain might come from the search algorithm itself, or it might come from a larger token budget, a stronger base model, or silently dropping timed-out tasks from the denominator. Judging any policy that combines candidate allocation, selection, verification checks, and early stopping therefore requires recording three things: the exact resource ceilings and permissions granted to each policy, the tokens, checks, and wall-clock time actually spent, and the fate of every task that failed to produce an accepted result.

### Controlled and system-level comparisons {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-comparison-design}

Comparing a multi-round search on a newer model against a single call on an older model, or counting only the tasks that finished before the deadline, mixes model capability and survivor bias with the effect of the search policy. A controlled policy comparison isolates the search policy by holding the base model, serving setup, benchmark tasks, tool interfaces, and acceptance criteria fixed while varying only the deliberation rule under the same resource ceilings and deadline. Prompt tokens, output tokens, check runs, and concurrency slots should each be stated as separate ceilings rather than folded into one vague "compute budget." Because a good policy stops early when a candidate passes, unspent budget reflects efficiency rather than an unfair test.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Complete agent policies are compared at matched budgets, with every initiated trial charged, by the method developed in @sec-vol3-evaluation-matched-budgets.
:::

A system-design comparison answers a broader engineering question: how two complete stacks trade cost, latency, and accuracy against one another. For instance, an engineer might compare one call to a large model against repeated calls to a smaller, faster model under the same dollar and latency caps. That comparison tells the team which stack to deploy, but it cannot separate the effect of search from the difference between the two models. Keeping controlled policy tests separate from stack-level comparisons prevents teams from crediting a model upgrade to their search algorithm.

Evaluation logs must record every started task, including explicit failures, abstentions, and deadline timeouts. To avoid crediting a search for exploiting its own scorer (the Goodhart failure of @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-selection-pressure), final output quality must be graded by an independent check rather than the internal score that guided the search. Logs should also separate three failure modes: false acceptance (returning a broken candidate), abstention or escalation, and deadline timeout. When reporting checker error rates, state the denominator explicitly.[^fn-false-discovery-rate] The share of broken candidates that pass a check ($\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate$) differs from the share of passing candidates that are broken ($1-\VerifierPrecision$). Furthermore, because sampling and branching are stochastic, benchmarks need repeated runs across the task set rather than a single point number.

[^fn-false-discovery-rate]: **Two Error Denominators**: The fraction of incorrect candidates that pass is the check's false positive rate, $\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate$ in this chapter; the fraction of accepted outputs that are incorrect is the false discovery rate, $1-\VerifierPrecision$. @Eq-vol3-verifier-precision connects them only through the valid-candidate rate, so a report that gives one without the base rate cannot be converted into the other. \index{False discovery rate!verifier reporting}

Total spend includes every resource used along the way: pruned branches, repeated prompt prefill across turns, verifier runs, and tokens decoded in flight after a cancellation signal. Dividing the total spend across the whole task cohort by the number of tasks that produced an accepted result gives the effective cost per accepted task, the cohort measure of $\CostPerAcceptedTask$ (@eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task). Because a slow repair that misses the service deadline is unusable, the share of tasks that finish before the deadline belongs right beside $\CostPerAcceptedTask$; a low average latency can hide a long tail where sequential revisions time out.

### Policies under a deadline {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-deadline-policies}

A deliberation policy that allows three feedback rounds on paper can run at most two rounds in practice when each round takes 30 seconds and the service deadline is 75 seconds. To see how concurrency limits and wall-clock deadlines constrain a policy in production, the notebook below compares three policies evaluated by a scoped test suite rather than an omniscient oracle. All probabilities are stipulated parameters chosen to show how concurrency, stopping rules, and token budgets interact under one deadline.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-deliberation-strategy
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THREE HYPOTHETICAL POLICIES UNDER A COMMON DEADLINE (LEGO)
# │ Goal: Compare completed suite-pass opportunities and actual expenditure.
# │ Show: Deadline-censored probability, expected tokens/checks, time, and bill.
# │ How: Fixed round allowance; independent breadth; conditional feedback gain.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check
from mlsysim.core.units import BYTES_INT8, dimensionless, param
import math

class StrategyComparison:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    accel = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    prompt = 2_048  # hypothetical fully serialized first request
    output = 1_000  # hypothetical generated tokens per candidate
    diagnostic = 340  # hypothetical failure-report tokens
    breadth = 8  # independent candidates, all generated and checked
    max_rounds = 3  # requested feedback cap, before deadline admission
    input_ceiling = 32_768
    output_ceiling = 8_192
    check_ceiling = 8
    concurrency = 8  # stipulated generator and check capacity
    deadline = 75 * second
    check_time = 10 * second  # distinct from earlier notebook scenarios
    initial_pass = 0.40  # scoped suite-pass probability for a fixed task
    revision_pass = 0.35  # conditional probability after a failed first attempt
    price_in = 3 * USD / 1_000_000  # hypothetical per-input-token price
    price_out = 15 * USD / 1_000_000  # hypothetical per-output-token price

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    weights = model.parameters / param * BYTES_INT8
    token_time = (weights / accel.memory.bandwidth).to(second)
    round_time = output * token_time + check_time
    rounds = min(max_rounds, math.floor((deadline / round_time).to(dimensionless).magnitude))
    first_cost = prompt * price_in + output * price_out
    revision_input = prompt + output + diagnostic
    revision_cost = revision_input * price_in + output * price_out
    a_pass = initial_pass
    b_pass = 1 - (1 - initial_pass) ** breadth
    c_pass = initial_pass + (1 - initial_pass) * revision_pass
    c_rounds = 1 + (1 - initial_pass)
    a_input, b_input = prompt, breadth * prompt
    c_input = prompt + (1 - initial_pass) * revision_input
    a_output, b_output, c_output = output, breadth * output, c_rounds * output
    a_cost, b_cost = first_cost, breadth * first_cost
    c_cost = first_cost + (1 - initial_pass) * revision_cost
    c_time = c_rounds * round_time
    max_c_time = rounds * round_time
    requested_time = max_rounds * round_time
    a_bill_per_pass = a_cost / a_pass  # model bill per suite-passing task
    b_bill_per_pass = b_cost / b_pass
    c_bill_per_pass = c_cost / c_pass
    b_over_a = (b_bill_per_pass / a_bill_per_pass).to(dimensionless).magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Validate Assumptions & Bounds) ─────────────────────────
    check(rounds == 2, "this notebook's conditional revision model has two rounds")
    check(0 <= initial_pass <= 1 and 0 <= revision_pass <= 1, "pass probabilities in [0, 1]")
    check(all(0 <= probability <= 1 for probability in (a_pass, b_pass, c_pass)), "probabilities in [0, 1]")
    check(max_c_time <= deadline < requested_time, "deadline bounds")
    check(prompt > 0 and output > 0 and diagnostic >= 0, "token counts positive")
    check(round_time > 0 * second and check_time >= 0 * second, "times non-negative")
    check(breadth <= min(concurrency, check_ceiling), "breadth within concurrency and check ceiling")
    check(rounds <= check_ceiling, "rounds within check ceiling")
    check(max(b_input, prompt + revision_input) <= input_ceiling, "input within ceiling")
    check(max(b_output, rounds * output) <= output_ceiling, "output within ceiling")
    check(a_bill_per_pass < c_bill_per_pass < b_bill_per_pass, "cost ordering")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Typed Prose Strings) ──────────────────────────────────
    prompt_str = fmt_int(prompt)
    output_str = fmt_int(output)
    diagnostic_str = fmt_int(diagnostic)
    breadth_str = fmt_int(breadth)
    rounds_str = fmt_int(rounds)
    max_rounds_str = fmt_int(max_rounds)
    input_ceiling_str = fmt_int(input_ceiling)
    output_ceiling_str = fmt_int(output_ceiling)
    check_ceiling_str = fmt_int(check_ceiling)
    concurrency_str = fmt_int(concurrency)
    deadline_str = fmt_time(deadline, unit="s", precision=0)
    check_time_str = fmt_time(check_time, unit="s", precision=0)
    token_time_str = fmt_time(token_time, unit="ms", precision=3)
    round_time_str = fmt_time(round_time, unit="s", precision=2)
    requested_time_str = fmt_time(requested_time, unit="s", precision=2)
    max_c_time_str = fmt_time(max_c_time, unit="s", precision=2)
    c_time_str = fmt_time(c_time, unit="s", precision=2)
    initial_pass_str = fmt_percent(initial_pass, precision=0, style="prose")
    revision_pass_str = fmt_percent(revision_pass, precision=0, style="prose")
    b_pass_str = fmt_percent(b_pass, precision=2, style="prose")
    c_pass_str = fmt_percent(c_pass, precision=0, style="prose")
    c_no_pass_str = fmt_percent(1 - c_pass, precision=0, style="prose")
    c_rounds_str = fmt_ratio(c_rounds, precision=1)
    price_in_str = fmt_usd(price_in * 1_000_000, precision=0)
    price_out_str = fmt_usd(price_out * 1_000_000, precision=0)
    a_input_str, b_input_str, c_input_str = fmt_int(a_input), fmt_int(b_input), fmt_ratio(c_input, precision=1, commas=True)
    a_output_str, b_output_str, c_output_str = fmt_int(a_output), fmt_int(b_output), fmt_int(c_output)
    a_cost_str, b_cost_str, c_cost_str = fmt_usd(a_cost, precision=5), fmt_usd(b_cost, precision=5), fmt_usd(c_cost, precision=5)
    a_per_pass_str = fmt_int(a_output / a_pass)
    b_per_pass_str = fmt_int(b_output / b_pass)
    c_per_pass_str = fmt_int(c_output / c_pass)
    a_bill_per_pass_str = fmt_usd(a_bill_per_pass, precision=4)
    b_bill_per_pass_str = fmt_usd(b_bill_per_pass, precision=4)
    c_bill_per_pass_str = fmt_usd(c_bill_per_pass, precision=4)
    b_over_a_mult_str = fmt_multiple(b_over_a, precision=1)
```

::: {#nbk-03-strategy-comparison .callout-notebook title="Three policies, one deadline"}

**Scenario**: Consider an automated software repair workload checked by a sealed regression suite. An initial candidate passes the suite with hypothetical probability $\AttemptPassProbability$ = `{python} StrategyComparison.initial_pass_str`, and repeated attempts on the same task draw candidates independently. Passing the suite is the acceptance rule for this stage, though passing tests does not guarantee that the patch is defect-free. Each policy runs under the same permissions and resource ceilings: at most `{python} StrategyComparison.input_ceiling_str` input tokens, `{python} StrategyComparison.output_ceiling_str` generated tokens, and `{python} StrategyComparison.check_ceiling_str` test runs, with up to `{python} StrategyComparison.concurrency_str` parallel workers and a hard `{python} StrategyComparison.deadline_str` deadline.

Each initial request sends `{python} StrategyComparison.prompt_str` prompt tokens, each candidate generates `{python} StrategyComparison.output_str` tokens, and running the test suite takes `{python} StrategyComparison.check_time_str`. Using the illustrative `{python} StrategyComparison.token_time_str` per-token decode time from @sec-vol3-foundation-model-per-call-work-estimate, assume that concurrent streams keep the same per-token rate and that tests run on dedicated workers without contention (omitting prefill, queueing, network transfer, and filtering overhead). Token prices are `{python} StrategyComparison.price_in_str` per million prompt tokens and `{python} StrategyComparison.price_out_str` per million output tokens, with no prefix-cache discount.

**Option A (single candidate)**: Generate and test one candidate. It passes the suite with probability `{python} StrategyComparison.initial_pass_str`, spending `{python} StrategyComparison.a_input_str` prompt tokens, `{python} StrategyComparison.a_output_str` generated tokens, and one test run. The attempt finishes in `{python} StrategyComparison.round_time_str` at a model bill of `{python} StrategyComparison.a_cost_str`, and if the test fails the runtime abstains.

**Option B (parallel breadth)**: Dispatch all `{python} StrategyComparison.breadth_str` candidates at once without early stopping, test each as it finishes, and return the first passing patch in index order. At least one of the $\CandidatePoolSize$ = `{python} StrategyComparison.breadth_str` candidates passes with probability pass@$\CandidatePoolSize = 1-(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^{\CandidatePoolSize}$ = `{python} StrategyComparison.b_pass_str`, which is also the chance of returning an accepted repair. Because all eight streams and tests fit within the concurrency limit, wall-clock time stays `{python} StrategyComparison.round_time_str`, while the fan-out spends `{python} StrategyComparison.b_input_str` prompt tokens, `{python} StrategyComparison.b_output_str` generated tokens, and `{python} StrategyComparison.breadth_str` test runs for a model bill of `{python} StrategyComparison.b_cost_str`.

**Option C (sequential feedback)**: Generate one candidate and stop right away if it passes. If it fails, append the failed patch and a `{python} StrategyComparison.diagnostic_str`-token failure trace to the prompt and request a revision, which passes with conditional probability $\RevisionPassProbability$ = `{python} StrategyComparison.revision_pass_str`. Although the policy nominally allows `{python} StrategyComparison.max_rounds_str` rounds, three sequential rounds would take `{python} StrategyComparison.requested_time_str` and miss the `{python} StrategyComparison.deadline_str` deadline. Only `{python} StrategyComparison.rounds_str` complete rounds fit inside `{python} StrategyComparison.deadline_str`, so the deadline caps the policy at one revision and forces an abstention if the second attempt also fails.

**Math**: With the third round cut off by the deadline, sequential feedback passes with probability $\AttemptPassProbability+(1-\AttemptPassProbability)\,\RevisionPassProbability$ = `{python} StrategyComparison.c_pass_str` and runs an expected $1+(1-\AttemptPassProbability)$ = `{python} StrategyComparison.c_rounds_str` rounds. Expected spend is `{python} StrategyComparison.c_input_str` prompt tokens, `{python} StrategyComparison.c_output_str` generated tokens, and `{python} StrategyComparison.c_rounds_str` test runs, for an expected model bill of `{python} StrategyComparison.c_cost_str` and an expected latency of `{python} StrategyComparison.c_time_str` (at most `{python} StrategyComparison.max_c_time_str`). The remaining `{python} StrategyComparison.c_no_pass_str` of tasks end without an accepted patch and must be counted as failed attempts. Across all started tasks, expected generated tokens per accepted repair are about `{python} StrategyComparison.a_per_pass_str` for Option A, `{python} StrategyComparison.b_per_pass_str` for Option B, and `{python} StrategyComparison.c_per_pass_str` for Option C.

**Systems insight**: Per accepted repair, the model bill is `{python} StrategyComparison.a_bill_per_pass_str` for Option A, `{python} StrategyComparison.c_bill_per_pass_str` for Option C, and `{python} StrategyComparison.b_bill_per_pass_str` for Option B (`{python} StrategyComparison.b_over_a_mult_str` the single-candidate baseline). Sequential feedback lifts the pass rate from `{python} StrategyComparison.initial_pass_str` to `{python} StrategyComparison.c_pass_str` at a small cost premium per accepted task, whereas parallel breadth reaches `{python} StrategyComparison.b_pass_str` at a much steeper bill per accepted repair.

The deadline decides which policy can run. When the service has room for only one `{python} StrategyComparison.round_time_str` round, parallel breadth is the only option here that improves on the `{python} StrategyComparison.initial_pass_str` single-call pass rate. When `{python} StrategyComparison.deadline_str` allows two rounds, sequential feedback raises the pass rate at a much smaller token bill than breadth, while a third round at `{python} StrategyComparison.requested_time_str` would never finish in time. In production, test-runner cost and false acceptance rates belong alongside the token bill so that passing the suite tracks real task fixes.

:::

### Choosing an operating point {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-operating-point}

No single policy in the comparison above wins on every axis: the single call is cheapest, parallel breadth finishes in one round at the highest pass rate, and two-round feedback reaches an intermediate pass rate at a much lower token bill than breadth. Each of the three sits on the Pareto frontier. A policy is strictly dominated only when another feasible policy matches or beats it on every metric (latency, token bill, checking load, and pass rate) and strictly beats it on at least one. Among non-dominated policies, the service's deadline, budget cap, and error tolerance pick the operating point.

Picking that operating point requires testing under the same limits the service will enforce in production. Analytical formulas cannot plug an ad-hoc "effective pool size" into pass@$\CandidatePoolSize$ when worker queues, prefix caching, and check runtimes reshape the actual cost and latency. Likewise, the gain from a feedback round depends on how informative the test failure trace actually is, and hard deadlines cut off multi-round searches before their planned final round. Benchmarks must therefore enforce the real worker timeouts, early-exit rules, and admission ceilings rather than extrapolating uncensored curves into a deadline-bound service.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-fallacies}

The most common mistakes in test-time compute come from treating extra work as proof of progress. Extra tokens, wider pools, and longer searches pay off only when the pool holds diverse hypotheses, the check separates valid repairs from plausible mistakes, and the budget account counts every discarded branch. When any of those pieces is missing, spending more compute only burns budget faster or selects more reliably for checker blind spots.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *More generated tokens necessarily produce a better answer.*

Extended reasoning can help a model trace constraints already present in the prompt, but it can just as easily elaborate and defend a wrong initial guess. When the open question concerns runtime behavior, generating tokens cannot supply the missing observation. In @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-insufficient-response, generating a `{python} ProbeAllocation.answer_tokens_str`-token explanation takes `{python} ProbeAllocation.answer_time_str`, `{python} ProbeAllocation.time_mult_str` the `{python} ProbeAllocation.probe_time_str` test run that directly separates the two hypotheses. Token count measures spend, not progress; extra reasoning tokens earn their keep only when benchmarks show they raise the accepted pass rate enough to justify their latency and cost.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Treating independent samples as independent capabilities.*

Samples drawn independently for a given prompt still share the same model weights and blind spots, so plugging a workload's average pass rate into pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$ overstates what breadth can deliver (@sec-vol3-test-time-compute-pass-at-k). Suppose half the tasks in a workload pass at `{python} BestOfN.p_easy_str` per candidate and the other half never pass ($\AttemptPassProbability = 0$). The average single-sample pass rate across the workload is `{python} BestOfN.p_str`, the same rate that notebook \ref{nbk-03-best-of-n-pool-price} used for a single task. Plugging that average into $1-(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^{\CandidatePoolSize}$ predicts `{python} BestOfN.naive_mix_str` success for a pool of `{python} BestOfN.n_max_str`, whereas the true success rate across the workload is only `{python} BestOfN.true_mix_str` because sampling never solves the half where $\AttemptPassProbability = 0$. Always compute pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$ per task first and average afterward.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *A check with a low false acceptance rate makes almost every pass trustworthy.*

How trustworthy a passing verdict is depends as much on the generator's base rate of valid candidates as on the check's error rates (@eq-vol3-verifier-precision). When valid candidates are scarce, even a small false acceptance rate lets broken candidates fill a large share of the passing pool. With a `{python} CheckYield.eps_fa_str` false acceptance rate, a `{python} CheckYield.eps_fr_str` false rejection rate, and a `{python} CheckYield.p_str` base rate of valid candidates, only `{python} CheckYield.precision_str` of passing candidates are valid, and a first-passing selector returns a broken repair on `{python} CheckYield.wrong_str` of task attempts (notebook \ref{nbk-03-compute-overhead-and-yield-under}). On hard tasks, raising the generator's base rate matters just as much for precision as tightening the check.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Charging only for the final answer.*

Pruned branches, repeated prompt prefill, test runs, and scorer calls all consume resources, and in-flight requests canceled at a deadline often keep billing until the remote server settles them. Pricing a deliberation policy by the tokens in its final returned answer hides most of its cost. In notebook \ref{nbk-03-strategy-comparison}, parallel breadth returns a single `{python} StrategyComparison.output_str`-token patch, but it bills `{python} StrategyComparison.b_output_str` output tokens per task and spends `{python} StrategyComparison.b_per_pass_str` output tokens per passing task. Likewise, the beam search in notebook \ref{nbk-03-compute-allocation-and-latency-trade-offs} reads `{python} SearchBudget.beam_prompt_tokens_str` input tokens to deliver `{python} SearchBudget.beam_width_str` final survivors. Production cost accounts must charge every discarded branch and failed attempt to the accepted tasks.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *The highest-scoring candidate has completed the task.*

A scorer orders candidates on whatever proxy it was built to measure, and picking the maximum score concentrates positive scoring errors into the winner. With equal true utilities and independent Gaussian noise, the winner among `{python} ArgmaxSelection.n_large_str` candidates has an expected scoring error of about `{python} ArgmaxSelection.shift_large_str` standard deviations (@eq-vol3-argmax-noise), and a checker loophole present in only `{python} ArgmaxSelection.gap_rate_str` of single candidates shows up in `{python} ArgmaxSelection.gap_present_str` of `{python} ArgmaxSelection.n_large_str`-candidate pools. A high relative score is neither a proof nor an authorization for properties the verifier did not test. When the budget runs out without a candidate passing the acceptance check, the top-scoring candidate is still an unverified failure.
:::

## Summary {#sec-vol3-ch3-summary}

Test-time compute turns the cost of a decision into an explicit runtime trade-off. While model weights fix what a single forward pass can do, the runtime chooses how much extra work to spend, whether to spend it on depth, breadth, or feedback, and what evidence justifies stopping. Extra deliberation lowers cost per accepted task only when three links all hold. Generation surfaces a valid candidate that a single call missed, the selector picks that candidate out of the pool, and the verifier checks the property the task actually requires. If any link fails, attempt cost rises while the acceptance rate $\AcceptanceProbability$ stalls, driving up $\CostPerAcceptedTask$. A deliberation policy should therefore be judged like any other systems component: by the accepted tasks it delivers per dollar and per second within the service deadline. @Tbl-vol3-test-time-compute-key-equations collects the equations derived in this chapter for pricing allocations, measuring pool availability and check precision, bounding search trees, and stopping early.

| **Equation**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   | **What it bounds or decides**                                                                                                                | **Where derived**                     |
|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------|
| $\DepthCriticalPathLatency \approx \PrefillTime(\SequenceLength) + \ExtendedDepthLength\,\PerTokenDecodeTime$, $\; \BreadthCriticalPathLatency \approx \PrefillTime(\SequenceLength) + \max_{n} \DecodeInterval(\OutputLength_n)$                                                                                                                              | Critical path of extending one candidate vs. sampling $\CandidatePoolSize$ concurrently, given capacity for all $\CandidatePoolSize$ streams | @eq-vol3-allocation-critical-path     |
| $\FeedbackCriticalPathLatency \approx \sum_{t=1}^{\TurnHorizon}\bigl(\PrefillTime(\SequenceLength^{(\TurnIndex)}) + \DecodeInterval(\OutputLength_t) + {\FeedbackCheckDuration}_{\TurnIndex}\bigr)$, $\; \SequenceLength^{(\TurnIndex)} = \BasePromptLength + \sum_{j<t}(\OutputLength_j + \lvert \TrajectoryObservation_j\rvert)$                             | Latency and input growth of observation-conditioned revision under an append-only context                                                    | @eq-vol3-allocation-critical-path     |
| $\operatorname{pass@}\IndependentAttemptCount = 1-(1-\AttemptPassProbability)^\IndependentAttemptCount$, $\; \PassAtKEstimate = 1-\binom{\GeneratedSampleCount-\PassingSampleCount}{\IndependentAttemptCount}/\binom{\GeneratedSampleCount}{\IndependentAttemptCount}$                                                                                         | Candidate availability for one task, and the ceiling on any selector that returns an unchanged pool member                                   | @sec-vol3-test-time-compute-pass-at-k |
| $\CostPerAcceptedTask = \mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]/\AcceptanceProbability$                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | How acceptance probability and expected attempt cost jointly determine cost per accepted task                                                | @eq-vol3-cost-per-accepted-task       |
| $\VerifierPrecision = \ValidCandidateRate(1-\VerifierFalseRejectionRate) / [\ValidCandidateRate(1-\VerifierFalseRejectionRate) + (1-\ValidCandidateRate)\,\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate]$                                                                                                                                                                       | Share of passing candidates that are valid; unchanged by pool size at fixed rates                                                            | @eq-vol3-verifier-precision           |
| $\sum_{j=1}^{\ScoredStepCount}(\SequenceLength + \ScoredStepIndex\,\FiniteChange \ScoredPrefixLength) = \ScoredStepCount \SequenceLength + \tfrac{\ScoredStepCount(\ScoredStepCount+1)}{2}\,\FiniteChange \ScoredPrefixLength$                                                                                                                                 | Scorer input for step-level checks that rescore each growing prefix without reuse                                                            | @eq-vol3-prm-rescoring                |
| $\mathbb{E}\bigl[\max_{i \le \CandidatePoolSize} \CandidateScoringError_i\bigr] \approx \ScoringErrorStandardDeviation\sqrt{2\ln \CandidatePoolSize}$, $\; 1-(1-\ExploitCandidateFraction)^\CandidatePoolSize$                                                                                                                                                 | Maximum-noise bound on the selected scoring error, and the chance a pool holds a check exploit                                               | @eq-vol3-argmax-noise                 |
| $\TreeSearchMeanReturn(\PolicyObservedState,\PolicyAction) + \TreeSearchExplorationWeight\,\TreeSearchPriorDistribution(\PolicyAction \mid \PolicyObservedState)\,\sqrt{\textstyle\sum_{\SiblingPolicyAction} \TreeSearchVisitCount(\PolicyObservedState,\SiblingPolicyAction)}\,/\,\bigl(1 + \TreeSearchVisitCount(\PolicyObservedState,\PolicyAction)\bigr)$ | Which extension of a partial candidate receives the next unit of tree search                                                                 | @eq-vol3-puct                         |
| $\EffectiveBranchingFactor = \SearchBranchingFactor\,(1 - \ChildPruningProbability)$, $\; \sum_{\SearchDepthIndex=1}^{\SearchDepth} \SearchBranchingFactor\,\EffectiveBranchingFactor^{\,\SearchDepthIndex-1}$                                                                                                                                                 | Whether pruning keeps a search tree finite, and the expected nodes it generates through depth $\SearchDepth$                                 | @eq-vol3-effective-branching          |
| $(\CalibratedAcceptanceEstimate_{\AdmittedWorkUnitCount} - \CalibratedAcceptanceEstimate_{\AdmittedWorkUnitCount-1})/(\CumulativeWorkCost_{\AdmittedWorkUnitCount} - \CumulativeWorkCost_{\AdmittedWorkUnitCount-1}) < \MarginalStoppingThreshold$                                                                                                             | Early stop after the hard-limit and satisficing checks, using incremental expected stopped-policy cost                                       | @eq-vol3-marginal-stopping            |

: **Key equations**: Each relation holds under the assumptions stated where it is derived, such as independent candidates for a fixed task, fixed checker error rates, and an unchanged per-token rate across concurrent streams. {#tbl-vol3-test-time-compute-key-equations tbl-colwidths="[46,36,18]"}

::: {.callout-takeaways title="More work needs a bounded policy"}

* **Observe when the question is empirical**: Generating more tokens re-examines what is already in the prompt, whereas running an external check brings in new runtime facts. In the connection-pool repair, generating one explanatory trace took `{python} ProbeAllocation.time_mult_str` as long as the targeted probe that separated the two hypotheses.
* **A pool is only as good as its selector**: Pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$ caps what an unchanged-member selector can return, not what it actually returns. Averaging pass rates across a mixed workload naively predicts `{python} BestOfN.naive_mix_str` success across `{python} BestOfN.n_max_str` candidates when the true pool delivers only `{python} BestOfN.true_mix_str`, because extra samples cannot solve tasks where the model has zero chance of success.
* **A pass inherits the base rate**: When valid candidates make up `{python} CheckYield.p_str` of the generator's output, a verifier with a `{python} CheckYield.eps_fa_str` false acceptance rate leaves only `{python} CheckYield.precision_str` of passing candidates valid. Under the fixed IID first-passing rule, returned candidates have that same precision regardless of pool size. With equal true utilities and independent Gaussian noise, picking the top score among `{python} ArgmaxSelection.n_large_str` candidates inflates the winner's score by about `{python} ArgmaxSelection.shift_large_str` standard deviations of noise.
* **Revise along recorded dependencies**: When an observation refutes an assumption, regenerate only the artifacts that depend on it rather than rebuilding the whole candidate plan. Missing dependency edges let stale conclusions survive silently, and plan revision never undoes side effects already committed to external systems.
* **Budgets end searches, not uncertainty**: Every pruned branch, verifier call, and failed attempt belongs in the cost per accepted task $\CostPerAcceptedTask$, and service deadlines bound how many sequential rounds can run. When a budget or deadline runs out without an accepted candidate, the runtime must abstain or escalate rather than returning the top-scoring unverified candidate.

:::

The verification asymmetry (principle \ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry})\index{Principle!verification asymmetry} gives a practical order for diagnosing any deliberation policy whose cost per accepted task is too high. First check pool availability per task via pass@$\CandidatePoolSize$. If passing candidates rarely enter the pool, switch to a stronger model or escalate rather than sampling wider. If the pass rate for a task is zero under the current prompt and model, more samples will not help. Where availability is healthy, check $\VerifierPrecision$ at the measured base rate, because a low precision means a better generator or a stricter check buys more than a larger pool. Only when both availability and precision are sound does the question become how many rounds of search to buy, which the marginal stopping rule answers in conditional acceptance gain per dollar. At every step, the runtime, not the model, decides whether to continue, abstain, or escalate.

## Historical Perspective and Further Reading {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-history}

Spending compute at decision time goes back to the earliest game-playing programs. Claude Shannon's 1950 design for a chess program separated generating candidate moves from scoring the resulting board positions with a heuristic evaluation function [@shannon1950programming]. Because game trees grow exponentially with depth, searching every branch to the end was impossible, and heuristic search—generating candidates and pruning weak branches with domain evaluations—became a central theme of artificial intelligence [@newell1976computer]. Beam search entered through speech recognition in HARPY [@lowerre1976], while the two stopping rules used in this chapter came from statistics and economics: Abraham Wald's sequential probability ratio test [@wald1945sequential] and Herbert Simon's satisficing [@simon1956rational].

Dependency-directed revision has an equally long history in systems and planning. Early robotics planners such as STRIPS and PLANEX checked plan preconditions against sensor readings and replanned when an observation contradicted an assumed state [@fikes1972learning]. Truth maintenance systems [@doyle1979truth] and `make` [@feldman1979make] turned that idea into the explicit dependency graphs that revisable candidate plans use today. As search spaces grew wider, Monte Carlo tree search [@coulom2006efficient; @kocsis2006bandit] introduced bandit-based tree expansion, and AlphaGo combined PUCT with neural policy and value networks to steer search through huge branching factors [@silver2016mastering].

Language models brought these search mechanisms together over text and code. In program synthesis, pass@$\IndependentAttemptCount$ measured how much parallel sampling improves functional test passage [@kulal2019spoc; @chen2021evaluating], and @cobbe2021training showed that training a separate verifier to rank sampled math solutions could beat scaling generator parameters alone. Chain-of-thought prompting extended depth within a single call [@wei2022cot], and self-consistency combined breadth with majority voting [@wang2022self]. Process supervision moved learned scoring from final answers to intermediate steps [@uesato2022solving; @lightman2023let], which enabled Tree of Thoughts [@yao2023tree] to run beam and tree search over multi-step reasoning.

More recent work treats test-time compute as an explicit budget to allocate across axes. @snell2024scaling showed that the best mix of sequential revision, parallel sampling, and verifier-guided search depends on task difficulty. Easy tasks favor revision, moderate tasks favor hybrid search, and tasks where the base model has near-zero success need a stronger model rather than more samples. Reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks then trained models to run long internal scratchpads that test ideas and backtrack inside a single generation [@deepseekai2025deepseekr1]. Finally, pushing search hard against learned reward models exposed Goodhart's law [@goodhart1984] in the form of reward-model overoptimization [@gao2023scaling], where the winner's proxy score keeps climbing while held-out accuracy peaks and falls.

- **Search as problem solving** [@newell1976computer]. Introduces heuristic search as generating and pruning hypotheses under resource limits, the framework that test-time compute policies build on.
- **Monte Carlo tree search** [@browne2012survey]. Surveys tree-search selection rules, rollouts, and backup operators adapted for multi-step language-model search.
- **Trained verifiers** [@cobbe2021training]. Shows that sampling candidates and ranking them with a trained verifier can beat scaling generator parameters alone.
- **Process supervision** [@lightman2023let]. Compares outcome-level and step-level supervision, detailing the labeling cost and pruning benefits of process reward models.
- **Reward-model overoptimization** [@gao2023scaling]. Measures how proxy reward scores diverge from held-out accuracy as best-of-$\CandidatePoolSize$ pool size grows.
- **Compute-optimal test-time allocation** [@snell2024scaling]. Analyzes how the frontier across parallel sampling, revision, and tree search shifts with task difficulty under a fixed compute budget.

## Exercises {#sec-vol3-test-time-compute-exercises}

Unless a problem states otherwise, use the hypothetical givens in @tbl-vol3-test-time-compute-exercise-givens. They are problem inputs chosen for round arithmetic, not measurements of any model or service. Omit prefill, queueing, and transport time, and apply no prefix-cache discount unless a problem introduces one.

| **Quantity**                                 | **Symbol**            | **Given**                 |
|:---------------------------------------------|:----------------------|:--------------------------|
| Generation time per output token, per stream | $\PerTokenDecodeTime$ | 20 ms                     |
| Generator input price                        |                       | \$3 per million tokens    |
| Generator output price                       |                       | \$15 per million tokens   |
| Learned-scorer input price                   |                       | \$0.50 per million tokens |

: **Givens for the exercises**: Hypothetical rates shared by the problems below. Concurrent streams keep the per-token rate up to the concurrency a problem states. {#tbl-vol3-test-time-compute-exercise-givens tbl-colwidths="[56,18,26]"}

**1. Three allocations, one repository (Basic).** A repair request carries an $8{,}000$-token prompt and a ceiling of $6{,}000$ generated tokens. Depth spends the whole ceiling on one candidate. Breadth generates six $1{,}000$-token candidates, but the service admits only three concurrent streams. Feedback runs $\TurnHorizon = 3$ rounds of $1{,}000$-token candidates; each round ends with a 6 s check that returns a 500-token report, and later requests append every earlier candidate and report.

(a) Using @eq-vol3-allocation-critical-path, compute each allocation's critical path, input tokens, output tokens, and model-token bill.
(b) The repository context grows to $64{,}000$ tokens. Recompute the three bills and the breadth premium $(\CandidatePoolSize-1)\SequenceLength$ in tokens and dollars.
(c) The task owner now requires a result within 60 s. Which allocation meets the deadline, and at what bill? A prefix cache would charge re-read prompt tokens at 10 percent of list price. What does breadth then cost, and what omitted term in this accounting should an engineer measure before committing to it?

**2. Sizing a pool against a target (Basic).** For a fixed repair task, independent candidates pass the acceptance check with probability $\AttemptPassProbability = 0.20$, and the selector returns a passing member whenever one exists.

(a) Find the smallest pool $\CandidatePoolSize$ whose pass@$\CandidatePoolSize$ reaches 90 percent, and the availability gained by its last candidate.
(b) Compare candidates spent per accepted repair for the parallel pool and for sequential retry that stops at the first pass and gives up after $\CandidatePoolSize$ attempts. What does the parallel pool buy for its premium?
(c) The workload is actually mixed: half the tasks pass at $0.40$ per candidate and half never pass, so the average rate is still $0.20$. What pool success does the pool size $\CandidatePoolSize$ from part (a) deliver, and what is the largest pool success any $\CandidatePoolSize$ can deliver? What should the runtime do with the second half of the workload instead?
(d) In a benchmark, 4 of 20 samples for one task pass. Compute the subset estimate of pass@5 and compare it with the plug-in value $1-(1-\PassingSampleCount/\GeneratedSampleCount)^5$.

**3. How strict must the check be? (Basic).** A candidate pool has valid-candidate rate $\ValidCandidateRate = 0.10$. The current check has $\VerifierFalseRejectionRate = 0.05$ and $\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate = 0.01$ and costs \$0.10 per run.

(a) Compute the probability of a pass $\VerifierPassProbability$ and the precision $\VerifierPrecision$ from @eq-vol3-verifier-precision.
(b) Precision must reach 95 percent. Find the largest $\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate$ that meets the target at this $\ValidCandidateRate$, and alternatively the smallest $\ValidCandidateRate$ that meets it with the current check.
(c) The policy pre-generates 32 candidates and checks them in a fixed order until the first pass, abstaining if none passes. Compute the probability of any selection, the probability that the batch contains at least one false pass, and the probability of selecting a defective candidate. Explain why the second and third differ.
(d) A stricter check has $\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate = 0.005$ and $\VerifierFalseRejectionRate = 0.08$ and costs \$0.40 per run. A defective selection costs \$2,000 in incident loss. Compare the two checks on expected incident loss plus expected checking cost per attempt, and decide which to deploy.

**4. What step scoring costs (Intermediate).** A learned process scorer reads a $3{,}000$-token task input and the growing prefix of a candidate built in $\ScoredStepCount = 20$ steps of 150 tokens each. The runtime scores 64 candidate trajectories per task at the scorer price in @tbl-vol3-test-time-compute-exercise-givens.

(a) Using @eq-vol3-prm-rescoring, compute scorer input per trajectory and per task when every prefix is rescored from scratch, and when the interface supports incremental prefix reuse.
(b) For this $\SequenceLength$ and $\FiniteChange \ScoredPrefixLength$, beyond how many steps does the quadratic term exceed the $\ScoredStepCount \SequenceLength$ term?
(c) Without prefix reuse, a team proposes scoring only every fourth step. Compute its scorer input and bill per task. A defective step is then caught on average 1.5 steps later, and every pruned trajectory generates those extra steps at the output price. Bound the added generation cost per task, and recommend a scoring stride with and without prefix reuse.

**5. Keeping a tree finite (Intermediate).** Each retained node proposes $\SearchBranchingFactor = 4$ children of 200 generated tokens, a step check rejects each child independently with probability $\ChildPruningProbability = 0.60$, and the search runs $\SearchDepth = 5$ steps deep under a ceiling of $20{,}000$ generated tokens.

(a) Compute $\EffectiveBranchingFactor$ from @eq-vol3-effective-branching and the expected generated nodes and tokens with and without pruning. Which expected counts fall below the ceiling, and why does an expected count below it not guarantee that every run fits?
(b) What rejection rate would make the tree die out on its own, and why is a rejection rate that high rarely available?
(c) The step check also rejects valid steps with probability $\VerifierFalseRejectionRate$. A correct solution needs five consecutive valid steps to survive. Compute its survival probability at $\VerifierFalseRejectionRate = 0.10$, and the largest $\VerifierFalseRejectionRate$ that keeps survival at or above 80 percent. What does this imply for tuning the check's threshold?

**6. A waiting customer sets the policy (Intermediate).** The support agent answers a policy question while the customer waits. Each request carries a $6{,}000$-token prompt of policy excerpts and conversation, each candidate reply is 150 output tokens, and a grounding check against the cited policy takes 1.5 s. A first reply passes with probability $0.70$; conditional on a failed first reply, a revision that reads the check's report passes with probability $0.50$. Concurrent candidates are checked concurrently, and the reply must arrive within 8 s.

(a) Compute the duration of one generate-and-check round. How many feedback rounds fit the deadline, and what pass probability does feedback therefore deliver?
(b) For concurrent breadth of $\CandidatePoolSize = 1$ to $4$, compute pass probability, model-token bill per request, and bill per passing reply. Find the smallest $\CandidatePoolSize$ that reaches 95 percent.
(c) The service can hold 600 concurrent decode streams for all sessions. How many simultaneous sessions does the choice in (b) support, compared with a single candidate? Which resource binds this policy?
(d) Contrast with the repair notebook (\ref{nbk-03-strategy-comparison}), where a second feedback round fit the deadline. Name the constraint that changed the answer, and state one design change that would make feedback viable for the support agent.

**7. Scoping a revision (Intermediate).** A repair candidate records generated artifacts. Each is listed here with its output tokens and direct prerequisites: diagnosis $\text{Dx}$ (300; source excerpt, failure observation), pool patch $\RepairPatchArtifact_1$ (600; source excerpt, $\text{Dx}$), metrics patch $\RepairPatchArtifact_2$ (200; $\text{Dx}$), check selection $\text{Chk}$ (150; $\RepairPatchArtifact_1$, test inventory), API notes $\text{API}$ (250; API declaration), release note $\text{Rel}$ (200; $\RepairPatchArtifact_1$, $\RepairPatchArtifact_2$, $\text{API}$), and migration script $\text{Mig}$ (400; $\text{API}$). The labels are local names for this problem only.

(a) A waiter-and-return test contradicts $\text{Dx}$. List $\text{Desc}(\text{Dx})$, and compute the output tokens of scoped regeneration (the diagnosis and its descendants) against full regeneration.
(b) Instead, the API declaration changes while the diagnosis stands. Which artifacts need review, and what share of the output does scoped regeneration avoid?
(c) The pool patch in fact calls the pool's public constructor, so $\RepairPatchArtifact_1$ depends on the API declaration, but that edge was never recorded. After the declaration changes, which stale artifacts survive the traversal, and what could the runtime then wrongly reuse? Propose how the runtime should record edges so that this failure cannot occur silently, and state what that costs.

**8. A judge under selection pressure (Advanced).** The research agent drafts $\CandidatePoolSize$ candidate summaries of what it has read, and a learned judge scores each as $\EstimatedCandidateUtility_i = \CandidateUtility_i + \CandidateScoringError_i$. True quality is $\CandidateUtility_i \sim \GaussianDistribution(\CandidateUtilityMean, \CandidateUtilityStandardDeviation^2)$ with $\CandidateUtilityStandardDeviation = 1.0$, scoring error is $\CandidateScoringError_i \sim \GaussianDistribution(0, \ScoringErrorStandardDeviation^2)$ with $\ScoringErrorStandardDeviation = 0.5$, all independent. The exact expected maximum of $\CandidatePoolSize$ standard normal draws is 1.03, 1.77, and 2.34 for $\CandidatePoolSize$ = 4, 16, and 64. Each candidate costs \$0.12.

(a) Using the exact values in place of @eq-vol3-argmax-noise, bound the winner's expected scoring error at each $\CandidatePoolSize$.
(b) Show that when selection is on $\EstimatedCandidateUtility$, the winner's expected quality gain over $\CandidateUtilityMean$ is $(\CandidateUtilityStandardDeviation^2/\EstimatedUtilityStandardDeviation)\,\ExpectedNormalMaximum$ and its expected error is $(\ScoringErrorStandardDeviation^2/\EstimatedUtilityStandardDeviation)\,\ExpectedNormalMaximum$, where $\EstimatedUtilityStandardDeviation = \sqrt{\CandidateUtilityStandardDeviation^2 + \ScoringErrorStandardDeviation^2}$ and $\ExpectedNormalMaximum$ is the expected standard-normal maximum. Evaluate both at the three pool sizes, and compare quality gained per dollar in moving from 4 to 16 and from 16 to 64 candidates.
(c) A fraction $\ExploitCandidateFraction = 0.002$ of summaries cite a retrieved page whose planted text the judge rewards but which does not support the claim. Compute the probability that a pool of 4, 16, and 64 contains at least one such summary, and explain why selection then tends to return it.
(d) Redesign the selection policy. Choose a pool size and a check the planted page cannot influence, and state what evidence the returned summary must carry. How does the binding constraint here differ from the repair agent's?

**9. Stopping before an irreversible change (Advanced).** The remediation agent generates candidate configuration changes in rounds, each costing \$0.20 in generation and a staging check. Calibrated on held-out incidents, the estimated probability of a staging-accepted candidate after $\AdmittedWorkUnitCount$ rounds is $\CalibratedAcceptanceEstimate_{\AdmittedWorkUnitCount}$ = 0.40, 0.58, 0.68, 0.74, 0.77, 0.79 for $\AdmittedWorkUnitCount$ = 1 to 6, with $\CalibratedAcceptanceEstimate_0 = 0$, and the hard ceiling is six rounds.

(a) For each prospective round, derive the conditional acceptance gain given no earlier pass and the increment in expected stopped-policy cost. Compute the marginal ratio of @eq-vol3-marginal-stopping. With $\MarginalStoppingThreshold = 0.25$ per dollar, how many rounds can the policy admit after earlier failures, and what are its acceptance probability and expected generation-and-check expenditure if it stops at the first accepted candidate?
(b) An accepted automated change saves \$30 of on-call time compared with escalation. Derive $\MarginalStoppingThreshold$ from that value, and state how many rounds the policy now admits and which rule ends the search.
(c) A colleague proposes that when the ceiling is reached without an accepted candidate, the agent applies its highest-scoring candidate. That candidate is defective with probability 0.5, a defective change costs \$40,000, and escalating to a human costs \$150. Compute each fallback's expected loss conditional on reaching the ceiling without an accepted candidate, then its contribution per initiated task under the policy in (a). Treat deliberation expenditure as common to both alternatives. Identify the stopping-precedence rule the proposal violates.
(d) Write the redesigned policy as the ordered checks the runtime applies before admitting another round, including what it returns in each case. Why does a staging-accepted candidate still not authorize the production change?

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From deliberation to working state"}
Deliberation leaves candidate versions, failed hypotheses, observations, and dependency records. The next model call cannot treat all of them as equally current or useful, even when every one of them still fits in its window. It needs a working context that retains the evidence supporting the selected candidate, distinguishes superseded material, and carries unresolved questions forward. @Sec-vol3-context-engineering develops this logical state-selection problem. Only after deciding what belongs in the working context does the physical question arise of how to store and reuse its model state, developed in @sec-vol3-kv-cache.
:::

```{=latex}
\part{key:vol3_memory}
```
